_note: Original top-up questions: every skill reaches at least 25 questions (Below / On / Above). Loaded by scripts/skills/top-up-skills.ts, which adds only what each skill is missing.

questions.stem: A poet wants to describe the ocean. Which line uses the sense of sound?
options: The ocean is very big and very blue.
I went to the beach with my family.
The sand is far away from the water.
The waves crash and hiss on the sand.

questions.stem: Which pair of words rhymes and could end two lines of a poem?
options: night / day
rain / cloud
night / bright
tree / branch
questions.why: Night and bright end with the same sound.

questions.stem: What is a stanza in a poem?
options: the poet's name at the top of a page in the book
the title of the poem on the cover of the book
a group of lines together, like a paragraph
one single word of the poem by itself on a line

questions.stem: Which line would make a good first line for a poem about autumn?
options: Red leaves spin like dancers in the wind.
Autumn is a season of the year.
There are four seasons in a year, as we know.
I have a lot of homework today and tomorrow.
questions.why: It paints a picture with vivid words.

questions.stem: A poet writes, "The moon is a silver coin." What did the poet use?
options: a metaphor
a list
a question
a rhyme
questions.why: It compares the moon to a coin without like or as.

questions.stem: Which word is the strongest choice for a poem about a storm?
options: roared
went
did
was
questions.why: Roared is vivid and shows power.

questions.stem: Which line repeats a sound at the beginning of words (alliteration)?
options: Birds fly high in the open sky.
The dog ran home after the walk.
I like my school and my class.
Silly snakes slide slowly.

questions.stem: What should a poet do first when writing a poem?
options: write the title last and never change anything after that
copy another poem word for word from a book
count the pages in the poetry book before starting
choose a topic and think of images and feelings about it

questions.stem: Which line uses a simile?
options: The kitten slept on the sofa.
The kitten is mine, not yours.
The kitten was as soft as a cloud.
The kitten has four legs and a tail.
questions.why: A simile compares with like or as.

questions.stem: A poet revises "The tree was nice" to make it stronger. Which revision is best?
options: The tree was very nice and very big.
The tree was really, really nice to see.
The old oak stretched its arms toward the sky.
There was a tree in the garden by the road.
questions.why: It adds a vivid image and personification.

questions.stem: Why might a poet break a line in the middle of a sentence?
options: to save paper in the book that is printed
because poems must have short lines on every page
to create a pause or put weight on a word
to make spelling easier for young readers
questions.why: Line breaks control rhythm and emphasis.

questions.stem: Which poem form has three lines with 5, 7 and 5 syllables?
options: sonnet
haiku
ballad
limerick

questions.stem: A poet wants readers to feel calm. Which line fits best?
options: The alarm screams at dawn.
Soft light rests on the quiet lake.
Thunder smashes the shaking house!
Hurry, hurry, run, run!
questions.why: Gentle words create a calm mood.

questions.stem: Which revision adds personification? "The wind blew through the town."
options: Blew the wind through the town at night.
The wind was in the town, and it stayed for a day.
The wind blew hard through the town.
The wind whispered secrets through the town.
questions.why: Whispering secrets gives the wind human actions.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of repeating a line at the end of each stanza?
options: to change the topic of the poem in each new stanza
to create a refrain that ties the poem together
to fill space at the end of the page
to confuse readers about the poem's meaning
questions.why: A refrain makes the poem musical and unified.

questions.stem: Which line shows, rather than tells, that someone is nervous?
options: She felt a feeling that she could not name.
Her hands trembled as she reached for the door.
She is a girl who lives in the town and goes to school.
She was nervous about it, and she knew it.

questions.stem: A free verse poem is a poem that—
options: has exactly 14 lines and a set rhyme at the end
is always funny and makes you laugh out loud
does not follow a set rhyme or rhythm pattern
must rhyme in every line of every verse and stanza
questions.why: Free verse has no fixed pattern.

questions.stem: A poet ends a poem about a grandfather's garden with "Each seed he planted still remembers his hands." What is the effect of this ending?
options: It describes the weather in the garden on that spring day.
It suggests his love and influence live on after him.
It lists the garden's plants and their names.
It explains how to plant seeds in the spring.
questions.why: The personified seeds show his lasting impact.

questions.stem: Which revision best tightens this line? "The very small little bird sang a very happy song."
options: The very little bird sang happily a song.
The wren sang its bright song.
The small little tiny bird sang.
The bird which was small sang a song that was happy.
questions.why: Precise nouns and fewer words make poetry stronger.

questions.stem: A poet uses short, choppy lines in a poem about a race. Why?
options: The poet ran out of ideas and decided to stop writing early.
The quick rhythm matches the speed and excitement of the race.
Short lines are easier to rhyme than long lines are.
Long lines are not allowed in any poem about sports.

questions.stem: Which line uses an extended metaphor across two lines?
options: I am worried today. / I am very tired tonight.
My worry is a heavy coat; / I carry it from room to room.
The sky is blue and wide. / The grass is green and soft.
Run fast, my friend. / Jump high in the air.
questions.why: The coat comparison continues in the second line.

questions.stem: A poet changes "I was sad when my friend moved" to "The swing beside mine sways empty now." Why is the revision stronger?
options: It names the friend who moved away to another town.
It is longer than the first sentence the poet wrote.
It uses a concrete image to show the feeling.
It rhymes with the line that comes before it.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the tone of these lines? "Gray streets, gray sky, / gray thoughts that will not fly."
options: gloomy
excited
cheerful
silly
questions.why: Repeated gray creates a gloomy tone.

questions.stem: In a sonnet, what often happens at the turn (volta)?
options: the rhyme stops completely for the last lines
the title changes into a different one
the poem shifts its idea or answers a problem
the poem ends suddenly without a final line
questions.why: The volta marks a shift in thought.

questions.stem: A poet wants the last word of a poem to surprise readers. Which technique helps most?
options: building expectations, then breaking the pattern at the end
using only one-syllable words in every line of the poem
repeating the title in every line of the poem
adding a footnote at the bottom of the page

questions.stem: Which source would give the most reliable facts about sharks?
options: a toy package from a shop
a friend's guess about sharks
a cartoon about sharks on TV
a book by a marine scientist

questions.stem: What is a keyword search?
options: drawing a picture of the website
reading every website on the internet
typing important words to find information
asking a stranger on the street for help
questions.why: Keywords help search engines find topics.

questions.stem: When you take notes for a report, you should—
options: write the main facts in your own words
write only your opinion about the topic
skip the source name and the page
copy every sentence from the book
questions.why: Notes in your own words avoid copying.

questions.stem: Why should you write down where you found a fact?
options: to make the report longer and look better
so you can give credit and find it again
because teachers like long lists of names
to hide the source from the reader
questions.why: Recording sources is honest and useful.

questions.stem: Which question is best to research for a short report on butterflies?
options: Are butterflies pretty, and are they colorful too?
What color is my shirt today, and why?
How do caterpillars become butterflies?
Do you like butterflies in your garden?
questions.why: It can be answered with facts.

questions.stem: Which website is probably most reliable for weather facts?
options: a national weather service site
a game site for kids to play online
a joke site with funny pictures
an ad for umbrellas and rain boots

questions.stem: What is a bibliography?
options: a story about a person's life and work
a list of the sources used in a report
a map of the places in a book
the report's title and the author's name

questions.stem: Which is a primary source?
options: a textbook summary
a movie review
an encyclopedia article written later
a diary written by a soldier during a war
questions.why: Primary sources come from people who were there.

questions.stem: A student finds two websites with different numbers for a mountain's height. What should the student do?
options: check a third reliable source to confirm
use both numbers in your report
pick the bigger number and ignore the other one
make up a new number that sounds right
questions.why: Confirming with more sources finds the accurate fact.

questions.stem: Which is the best paraphrase of "Honeybees communicate the location of flowers through a dance"?
options: Bees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
Honeybees communicate the location of flowers through a dance.
Dancing is fun for bees.
Bees like flowers.
questions.why: A paraphrase keeps the meaning in new words.

questions.stem: Why is copying a writer's sentences without credit a problem?
options: It is plagiarism—using someone's work as your own.
It makes the report too short for the teacher.
It is always allowed online, if you copy it exactly.
It is against the spelling rules of the school.

questions.stem: Which detail suggests a website may NOT be reliable?
options: It was updated recently by a known writer.
It has no author and many spelling errors.
It lists its sources at the bottom of the page.
It is from a university in a big city.
questions.why: No author and errors are warning signs.

questions.stem: A student researching volcanoes finds a fact about earthquakes. What should the student ask?
options: Is it funny enough to make my class laugh?
Does this fact help answer my research question?
Does it have pictures that look nice on the page?
Is this fact long enough to fill a whole page?

questions.stem: Which is a secondary source about the first moon landing?
options: a magazine article written years later
a recording of the astronauts' voices
an astronaut's own mission journal
a photo taken on the moon

questions.stem: What is the best way to organize notes from several sources?
options: keep them in the order you found them
throw away the ones you don't like
put them all in one sentence
group them by subtopic
questions.why: Grouping by subtopic helps write sections.

questions.stem: A student quotes an expert. What must the student include?
options: nothing extra
only the first word
the student's opinion inside the quote
quotation marks and the expert's name

questions.stem: A student's source is a website run by a company that sells the product it reviews. What should the student consider?
options: Company sites never contain facts, only advertisements.
The site may be biased because it profits from sales.
Bias does not matter in research, only the topic does.
The site is always more accurate than a book or a library.
questions.why: A financial interest can create bias.

questions.stem: Which research question is too narrow for a five-page report?
options: Why are libraries important to communities around the world?
How did public libraries change in the 1900s?
What year was the town's first library card printed?
How do libraries help students learn to read better?
questions.why: A single date cannot fill a report.

questions.stem: A student finds an article from 1995 about cell phones. Why might it be a weak source for current facts?
options: It has no pictures.
The information is outdated.
Old articles are always wrong about everything.
It is too short.

questions.stem: Which citation is most complete?
options: Lopez, Ana. "Desert Plants." Science Today.
Science Today, 2024, a science magazine for students, page 12.
Ana wrote it, and it is in a science magazine.
Lopez, Ana. "Desert Plants." Science Today, 2024, p. 12.
questions.why: It gives author, title, publication, year and page.

questions.stem: Two sources disagree about why a city grew. How should a strong report handle this?
options: explain both views and which has stronger evidence
ignore both sources and write nothing about it
choose the source with more pictures in the book
copy both texts and hand them in as one

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of synthesizing sources?
options: listing websites that you found on the internet and their names
combining information from several sources to form new understanding
choosing only one source and ignoring all the others
copying one source carefully, word for word, into your notes

questions.stem: Which search would find the most focused results about coral bleaching in Australia?
options: "coral bleaching" Great Barrier Reef causes
Australia beaches and travel guide
ocean animals and plants in the sea
fish and coral and water and sea and ships
questions.why: Specific keywords and quotation marks focus results.

questions.stem: What should the beginning of a story do?
options: give the moral only and nothing else
list facts about the real world
tell the ending to the reader at once
introduce the characters and setting

questions.stem: Which word helps show the order of events in a story?
options: next
because
but
very

questions.stem: Which sentence uses dialogue?
options: Lina waited for the bus.
Lina ran home after school.
"Wait for me!" called Lina.
Lina is my friend from school.

questions.stem: What is the problem in a story also called?
options: the title
the conflict
the author
the setting

questions.stem: Which detail best describes a setting?
options: Sam was happy about his new bike and shoes.
The end of the story came soon.
He said hi to the girl next door.
The dusty road wound past empty fields.
questions.why: It tells where the story happens.

questions.stem: Which ending gives the story a sense of closure?
options: At last, the lost puppy was home, curled up by the fire.
And then, a new problem began for the puppy.
The story is about a puppy that got lost in a park.
Something happened to the puppy, but nobody knows what.

questions.stem: What does a narrator do?
options: draws the pictures
sells the book
prints the book
tells the story

questions.stem: Which sentence shows a character's feeling through action?
options: Omar was angry with his brother for a long time.
Omar stomped up the stairs and slammed his door.
Omar is a boy who lives in the town and goes to school.
Omar lives here with his mother and his aunt.

questions.stem: Which revision makes this sentence more vivid? "The dog ran."
options: A dog was running in the yard near the house.
The dog ran fast across the yard to the gate.
The dog ran and ran until it was very tired.
The scruffy dog bolted across the muddy yard.

questions.stem: A writer wants to slow down an exciting moment. What should the writer do?
options: write one short sentence and stop writing for the day
skip to the end of the scene quickly, to save time
change the topic to a new one in the next line
add sensory details and the character's thoughts

questions.stem: Which transition shows a jump in time?
options: Also,
Three days later,
For example,
In addition,

questions.stem: Which is first-person point of view?
options: She grabbed her bag and ran.
I grabbed my bag and ran.
They ran home.
He was late.

questions.stem: What makes a narrative's conflict interesting?
options: nothing goes wrong for the character in the story
there are no characters in the story at all
the character wants something and faces obstacles
the setting is described only, with no events

questions.stem: Which line of dialogue best reveals a character's personality?
options: "Rules? I make my own rules," Zain smirked.
"Hello," said Zain.
"Yes," said Zain.
"Okay," said Zain.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best hook for a story?
options: Once there was a day when a boy went out to play in the park and met a dog.
I will tell you about a river that is near my home, and about my uncle.
This is a story about a small town and its people and what they did there.
The day the river turned purple, nobody in Elm Town could explain it.

questions.stem: Why might a writer begin a story in the middle of the action?
options: to confuse readers forever and make them stop reading it
to make it shorter than the other stories are
because beginnings are not needed in a book or tale
to grab the reader immediately and build suspense

questions.stem: Which revision uses pacing to build suspense?
options: The door opened and someone walked in slowly and sat down.
There was a door in the house.
Someone came in.
The door creaked. Silence. Then—footsteps.
questions.why: Short fragments slow the moment and build tension.

questions.stem: A writer includes a flashback. What must the writer make clear?
options: the page number of the flashback scene
the title of the story and the author
when the story moves to the past and back
the moral of the story and its message

questions.stem: Which ending best shows how the main character has changed?
options: Maya liked school, and she went there every day with her best friends and her cousin.
This time, Maya raised her hand first—no shaking voice, no second thoughts.
The day was over, and the sun went down behind the buildings.
Maya went home, ate her dinner and watched TV with her mother.
questions.why: It contrasts with her earlier fear.

questions.stem: What is the effect of writing a narrative in present tense?
options: It makes events feel immediate, as if happening now.
It makes the story about the future, not the past.
It removes all action from the story.
It turns the story into a poem with rhymes.

questions.stem: Which detail is LEAST useful in a story about a girl's first swim race?
options: her heart pounding on the starting block
the cheers from the stands
the price of bread at the bakery
the cold splash of the water
questions.why: It does not develop the story.

questions.stem: A writer reveals a character's thoughts through an unreliable narrator. What does this create?
options: a list of facts that the narrator gives to us
a clear summary of the whole plot in the first chapter
doubt about what is really true, making readers think
a recipe that explains how to make bread
questions.why: Unreliable narrators create tension and questions.

questions.stem: Which sentence states an opinion?
options: Our school has a playground.
Recess should be longer.
Recess is at 10 o'clock.
There are 30 students in my class.

questions.stem: Which reason best supports "Students should read every day"?
options: The library is big and very quiet.
Reading every day builds vocabulary.
Books have covers with nice pictures.
Some books are red and some are blue.

questions.stem: Which word introduces a reason?
options: then
next
finally
because

questions.stem: What should the conclusion of an opinion piece do?
options: ask the reader to stop reading
list random facts
start a new topic
restate the opinion

questions.stem: Which is a fact, not an opinion?
options: Cold days are boring.
Winter is the best season.
Water freezes at 0 °C.
Snow is fun.

questions.stem: Which opinion sentence is clearest?
options: Gardens, maybe, could be something.
I don't know about gardens.
Plants exist.
Our class should plant a school garden.

questions.stem: Which detail supports "Pets make good companions"?
options: Pets can help people feel less lonely.
Pet stores are open on Monday morning.
Pets have names, like Max or Luna.
Some pets are small, like birds.
questions.why: It explains why pets are good companions.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence is strongest for "Schools should serve healthy lunches"?
options: I like salad, and I eat it with my lunch every day at school.
Lunch is at noon, and it lasts for thirty minutes in our school.
A study found students who eat healthy lunches focus better in class.
My friend eats pizza for lunch on most days of the week.

questions.stem: What is a counterclaim?
options: an opposing argument the writer answers
the writer's main claim in the first paragraph
the title at the top of the page
a list of sources at the end of the text

questions.stem: Which transition best introduces a counterclaim?
options: For example, a boy who
Some people argue that
In conclusion, then we see
Finally, at the last

questions.stem: Which sentence best responds to the counterclaim "Homework takes away free time"?
options: I don't care about free time, so I do not mind the homework.
Homework is homework, and that is all there is to it.
That is wrong, and the writer should say sorry to the class.
However, short daily homework builds habits that save time later.
questions.why: It answers the counterclaim with a reason.

questions.stem: Which claim is most arguable (people could disagree)?
options: Video games can help students learn.
Video games were invented in the 1900s.
Video games use electricity.
Video games have screens.

questions.stem: Why should a writer explain how evidence supports a claim?
options: so readers see the connection
to make the essay longer
to change the claim
because evidence explains itself always

questions.stem: Which tone is best for a persuasive letter to the principal?
options: confused
rude and angry
silly and joking
respectful and confident

questions.stem: Which sentence is a precise, arguable claim?
options: Some people like projects more than tests and quizzes in class.
School is a place where children learn and play together every day of the week.
Our school should replace one weekly test with a project to deepen learning.
Tests are bad for kids who work hard every day at school and home.

questions.stem: A writer uses the statement "Everyone knows phones are harmful." What is weak about it?
options: It is too specific, with many small details in it.
It is a sweeping generalization without evidence.
It quotes an expert in the field of health and sleep.
It uses a statistic from a trusted survey of schools.

questions.stem: Which evidence is most credible for an argument about air pollution?
options: a cousin's opinion about the traffic near us
data from an environmental protection agency
a comment on a social media post by a friend
a slogan on a poster in a shop window

questions.stem: What does it mean to rebut a counterclaim?
options: to ignore it and pretend it is not there
to agree with it completely and change your claim
to explain why the opposing argument is weaker
to repeat it again in the same words
questions.why: A rebuttal answers the other side.

questions.stem: Which revision avoids an emotional appeal and uses logic instead?
options: Imagine the tears of families who lost loved ones!
Bike lanes are awesome!
Only cruel people oppose bike lanes.
Bike lanes reduced accidents by 30% in nearby cities.

questions.stem: A writer's conclusion includes a call to action. What does that mean?
options: it adds new evidence
it summarizes the counterclaim only
it changes the claim
it asks readers to do something specific
questions.why: A call to action urges response.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to organize an argument essay?
options: counterclaim only, with no claim at the start and no end to it
evidence only, with no reasons or claim to explain it all
conclusion first, then random facts and a claim at last, in a row
claim, reasons with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion

questions.stem: What is the purpose of informative writing?
options: to share only opinions about the topic
to make readers laugh at a funny tale
to tell a made-up story about a hero
to teach or explain facts about a topic

questions.stem: Which sentence is a good topic sentence for a paragraph about frogs?
options: The end of the book is here.
Do you like frogs or toads?
Frogs have amazing ways to survive.
I saw a frog once at the pond last year.

questions.stem: Which detail belongs in a paragraph about how plants grow?
options: Plants need sunlight and water.
Winter is cold in the north.
My sister likes pizza very much.
Cars need gas to run well.

questions.stem: Which text feature helps readers find sections?
options: jokes
dialogue
rhymes
headings

questions.stem: Which word introduces an example?
options: for example
however
but
finally

questions.stem: Which sentence defines a term?
options: I like habitats because they are so interesting.
The word habitat starts with the letter h.
A habitat is the place where an animal lives.
Habitats are cool places to visit in summer.
questions.why: It explains what the word means.

questions.stem: What should an informative conclusion do?
options: ask readers to stop reading
sum up the main points
add a new topic or idea
tell a joke to the readers

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a precise, domain-specific word?
options: The volcano did things.
The volcano released molten lava.
The volcano let out hot stuff.
The volcano was big and bad.

questions.stem: A writer explains how to make a kite. Which structure fits best?
options: sequence (step by step)
problem and solution
cause and effect
compare and contrast

questions.stem: Which transition shows a contrast between two facts?
options: Next, after that,
On the other hand,
First, of all,
Also, as well,

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that camels survive in deserts?
options: Some camels live in zoos in the big cities of the world.
Camels have names like Sahm or Noor, given by their owners.
Camels are tall and have long legs and a small tail.
Camels can go many days without drinking water.

questions.stem: Why might a writer add a diagram to an explanation of the water cycle?
options: to make the report funny
to add an opinion
to replace all the text
to show the steps visually

questions.stem: Which sentence keeps a formal style?
options: Rivers are super gross, lol.
Scientists study the effects of pollution on rivers.
Scientists totally check out rivers and stuff.
Science people look at water.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to group facts in an essay about the planets?
options: by planet, with one paragraph each
all in one sentence, with no breaks
in the order you found them in books
randomly, with no plan at all

questions.stem: Which thesis is strongest for an essay about recycling?
options: Recycling conserves resources, saves energy and reduces landfill waste.
I recycle sometimes, when there is a bin near my house.
This essay is about recycling and what I think about it.
Recycling is a thing that people do in some towns and in some homes.

questions.stem: A writer explains the causes of a famine. Which organization fits?
options: cause and effect
compare two recipes
chronological story of a hero
poem

questions.stem: Which sentence best integrates a quotation?
options: Bees pollinate many crops, and then the quote is added after this sentence.
"Bees pollinate a third of our crops." Bees are important to farmers and to us all.
According to biologist Dr. Reem Said, "Bees pollinate a third of our crops."
Dr. Said said bees something about crops, but the quote is not shown.

questions.stem: Which revision removes unnecessary information from an essay on solar energy?
options: Delete the statistic on energy savings in the home.
Delete the definition of solar panels from the start.
Delete the sentence about the writer's favorite movie.
Delete the topic sentence of the first paragraph.

questions.stem: Why should a writer anticipate the reader's questions?
options: to shorten the essay and use fewer words
to make the essay confusing and hard to follow
to answer them and make the explanation complete
to add opinions that have nothing to do with the topic

questions.stem: Which sentence best concludes an essay on ocean plastic?
options: Reducing single-use plastic today can protect ocean life for generations.
Plastic is a word that we hear and use every day at home and at school.
That is all I have to say about plastic in the ocean for today.
Oceans are very big, deep and blue in many parts of the whole world.

questions.stem: Which detail is most precise?
options: About 8 million tons of plastic enter the oceans each year.
Some plastic is bad for the sea and also bad for fish.
Plastic is everywhere, in the shops and in the streets and parks.
A lot of plastic goes into the ocean each year, many people say.

questions.stem: In "The baseball player swung the bat," what does bat mean?
options: a wooden stick used in sports
a flying animal that lives in caves
a small hat that children wear
to blink your eyes very fast
questions.why: A player swings a wooden bat.

questions.stem: In "We saw a bat flying at night," what does bat mean?
options: a turn in a game
a kind of cap
a flying animal
a stick for hitting a ball
questions.why: Flying at night tells us it is an animal.

questions.stem: In "Please wave goodbye," what does wave mean?
options: a moving ridge of water in the sea
move your hand back and forth
a sudden feeling of joy or fear
a curl in hair on the head
questions.why: You wave your hand to say goodbye.

questions.stem: In "The ring on her finger sparkled," what does ring mean?
options: a circle where boxers fight
the sound of a bell
to call on the phone
jewelry worn on a finger

questions.stem: In "The bark of the tree was rough," what does bark mean?
options: the outside covering of a tree
a kind of boat that sails the sea
to shout in a loud voice
the sound a dog makes at night

questions.stem: In "Turn on the light," what does light mean?
options: a lamp or brightness
to start a small fire
not heavy at all, but
pale in color or in tone

questions.stem: In "The box was light enough to carry," what does light mean?
options: not heavy
bright
a lamp
early morning
questions.why: Easy to carry means not heavy.

questions.stem: In "The coach will train the team," what does train mean?
options: teach and practice skills
a line of railway cars
the long part of a dress
a row of animals

questions.stem: In "She will file the papers," what does file mean?
options: put in order and store
a metal tool for smoothing
a line of people
a computer game

questions.stem: Which sentence uses fair to mean "a festival with rides and games"?
options: The rules were fair to everyone in the game.
The weather will be fair on the weekend.
She has fair skin and light brown hair.
We rode the Ferris wheel at the fair.
questions.why: Rides and games happen at a fair.

questions.stem: In "The pitcher threw a fast ball," which other meaning of pitcher does NOT fit?
options: a baseball position
a jug for pouring water
the player who throws the ball
a team member
questions.why: Here pitcher is a player, not a jug.

questions.stem: In "Don't bear the weight alone," what does bear mean?
options: carry or support
bare, uncovered
a large furry animal
to give birth
questions.why: Bear the weight means carry it.

questions.stem: In "Mom made a match between the two socks," what does match mean?
options: a small stick that makes fire
a pair that goes together
a sports game
to compete

questions.stem: In "The scientist will present her findings," what does present mean?
options: now, at this time of the day
in attendance at a school party
show or explain to an audience
a gift given on a birthday

questions.stem: Which sentence uses object as a verb meaning "to disagree"?
options: Every object has a shape.
The object of the game is to win.
I object to that unfair rule.
The object on the table is a cup.
questions.why: Object as a verb means oppose.

questions.stem: In "The general feeling was hopeful," what does general mean?
options: not detailed or exact
shared by most people
a store that sells food
an army officer of high rank
questions.why: General feeling means most people's feeling.

questions.stem: Which clue word helps you know the meaning of seal in "The seal balanced a ball on its nose"?
options: the, balanced a ball on
balanced a ball on its nose
its nose and its ball and
ball on its nose, too, yes
questions.why: That action points to the animal.

questions.stem: In "The novel had a strong plot," which meaning of novel fits?
options: new and unusual, like an idea
a long book that tells a story
a small notebook for writing notes
a type of plant that grows in gardens

questions.stem: In "The idea was novel, so no one had tried it," what does novel mean?
options: new and unusual
boring
a long story
old-fashioned
questions.why: No one had tried it, so it was new.

questions.stem: What is foreshadowing?
options: the title of the story that is on the cover
a list of characters at the start of a play
the end of a story, where it all finishes
a hint about something that will happen later
questions.why: Foreshadowing gives clues about later events.

questions.stem: Dark clouds gather as the hikers start up the mountain. What might this foreshadow?
options: a storm or trouble ahead
a birthday party soon at home
a quiet nap later on
a sunny picnic for all
questions.why: Dark clouds hint at a storm.

questions.stem: A character says, "I have a bad feeling about this." What does this do?
options: tells a joke to make people laugh
describes the setting of the scene
hints that something will go wrong
ends the story with a happy sentence

questions.stem: In a story, a boy notices a loose board on a bridge. Later, he trips there. The loose board was—
options: the title
the theme
foreshadowing
a flashback
questions.why: It hinted at the later event.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an example of foreshadowing?
options: Lina's coat was blue and warm that day, in winter.
Lina skated every winter on the pond near her home.
Lina lived in town near the lake with her aunt.
Lina didn't notice the cracked ice near the shore.
questions.why: The cracked ice hints at danger.

questions.stem: Why do authors use foreshadowing?
options: to build suspense and prepare readers
to end chapters with a happy ending
to list facts about the characters
to make stories shorter and easier to finish

questions.stem: A dog growls at a new visitor at the start of a story. What could this hint?
options: the visitor may not be trustworthy
the story is over and the dog sleeps
the dog is hungry and wants food
it is raining outside and the dog is wet
questions.why: The dog's reaction hints at the visitor.

questions.stem: At the start of a story, Grandpa gives Mia an old compass "just in case." Later she gets lost. How does the compass work in the plot?
options: It is the theme of the whole story.
It is a flashback to the past.
It foreshadows that she will need it.
It describes the setting only, not the plot.
questions.why: The gift hints she will need it.

questions.stem: Which detail most likely foreshadows a surprise ending?
options: The neighbor had a red car that he washed on Sundays.
The street was long, with trees on both sides of it.
The quiet neighbor always kept his garage door locked.
It was Tuesday, and the sun was shining all day.
questions.why: A locked secret hints at a reveal.

questions.stem: How is foreshadowing different from a flashback?
options: Foreshadowing hints at the future; a flashback shows the past.
A flashback hints at the future of the hero in a tale or a film.
They are the same thing in a story, with the same effect on the reader.
Foreshadowing shows the past of the hero in a story or a film.
questions.why: They point in opposite directions in time.

questions.stem: A chapter ends: "If only she had read the last line of the letter." What does this create?
options: a summary of what the girl did last week
a definition of the word letter in a book
suspense about what the letter said
a conclusion that ties up all of the story
questions.why: Readers want to know what happens.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence that an event was foreshadowed?
options: An earlier detail hinted that it would happen.
The event had many characters in the story.
The event was exciting and very fast.
The event happened at night in the dark.
questions.why: Foreshadowing is shown by earlier hints.

questions.stem: Mysterious music plays when a character opens a door in a film. This is like foreshadowing because—
options: it ends the movie and tells the viewers to go home
it names the character and tells us his age and job
it signals that something important or scary will happen
it shows the past and explains what happened last year

questions.stem: An author mentions a broken lock three times early in a mystery. What is the most likely purpose?
options: to plant a clue that will matter in the solution
to introduce a new character late in the story
to describe the weather in the village that night
to fill space in the middle of the book

questions.stem: How can foreshadowing make an ending feel satisfying rather than random?
options: It changes the narrator in the middle of the whole text.
It hides all the clues from the readers until the end.
Earlier hints make the ending feel earned and believable.
It removes the suspense from the story for good, too.
questions.why: Hints prepare readers for the outcome.

questions.stem: A story's first line is "Nobody in the village believed the old warning about the river." What does it foreshadow?
options: that the village is happy and safe
that the river is dry in summer
that nothing will happen to anyone
that the warning will come true

questions.stem: Which is an example of a 'red herring' rather than true foreshadowing?
options: a description of the setting in the first chapter
the title of the book printed on the cover
a clue that misleads readers toward the wrong suspect
a hint that correctly predicts the ending of the story

questions.stem: In a tragedy, the hero says, "Nothing can stop me now." What does this line likely foreshadow?
options: a happy wedding
a new setting
his downfall
his success forever
questions.why: Overconfidence often hints at a fall.

questions.stem: Why might an author foreshadow subtly instead of obviously?
options: to make the story longer than it was when it started
because foreshadowing is not allowed in books for kids
to surprise readers while keeping the ending believable
to confuse readers forever and ever and ever
questions.why: Subtle hints balance surprise and logic.

questions.stem: What is a pun?
options: a long story with many chapters and many characters
a joke that plays on words with two meanings or similar sounds
a rhyme only, used in songs for very small children
a kind of poem with 14 lines and a strict rhyme pattern at the end

questions.stem: Why is this a pun? "The math book looked sad because it had too many problems."
options: Math is hard, and many students do not like it.
Books can talk, so the book told the class it was sad.
Sad rhymes with bad, and both words end the same.
Problems means math questions and also troubles.
questions.why: The word problems has two meanings.

questions.stem: "I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough." What two meanings does dough have?
options: bread mix and money
money and time at a bank
water and flour in a bowl
bread and cake at a shop

questions.stem: Which sentence is a pun?
options: I ride my bicycle to school with my friends every day.
The bicycle fell over because it was two-tired.
The bicycle is red and has a small bell.
Bicycles have wheels, pedals and a seat.

questions.stem: "Why did the cookie go to the doctor? It felt crummy." What makes it funny?
options: Cookies are sweet, and sweet things are funny.
Doctors like cookies, so they eat them often.
Crummy means full of crumbs and also feeling bad.
It rhymes, and the two lines sound the same.

questions.stem: Which word is used for wordplay in "Time flies like an arrow"?
options: an
flies
like
time
questions.why: Flies can mean moves fast or insects.

questions.stem: A pun usually makes readers—
options: fall asleep during the long, quiet lesson
feel scared, as if something bad is near
cry because the joke is sad for them
laugh or groan at a clever double meaning

questions.stem: "The scarecrow won an award because he was outstanding in his field." Explain the pun.
options: Crows are scared of scarecrows, and that is the joke.
Fields are large and flat, and farmers need many of them to grow food.
Outstanding in his field means excellent and standing in a field.
Scarecrows win awards for being good at scaring crows.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a homophone pun?
options: The castle was tall and made of gray stone.
It was night, and the moon was bright.
The knight was afraid of the dark night.
The knight rode a horse across the field.

questions.stem: What makes this wordplay? "A boiled egg in the morning is hard to beat."
options: It rhymes with the line before it in the poem.
Eggs are boiled in water for a few minutes.
Morning is early, and many people are asleep.
Hard to beat means excellent, and eggs are beaten.

questions.stem: Why do writers use puns in titles of articles?
options: to make titles longer than the text
to catch readers' attention with humor
to hide the topic from the readers
to give exact facts and dates only

questions.stem: "I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. It's impossible to put down." What is the pun?
options: Gravity is strong, and so the book falls fast to the floor.
Reading is fun, and so the book is a nice one too.
Books are heavy, so it is hard to put down a book.
Impossible to put down means very interesting and won't fall.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an example of wordplay?
options: The river flows to the sea.
I'm on a seafood diet: I see food and eat it.
Bakers knead the dough they need.
Seven days without a pun makes one weak.

questions.stem: "Seven days without a pun makes one weak." What two meanings are combined?
options: seven and one more day
one week and one weak person
days and nights of the week
pun and fun in one word

questions.stem: In a play, a dying character says, "Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man." What is the effect of the pun?
options: It is only a fact about a man who is ill in bed at home.
It describes the weather in the town at night in the cold winter.
It mixes humor with the seriousness of death (grave = serious / tomb).
It introduces a new setting for the next scene of the play, in a church.
questions.why: Grave has two meanings, adding dark humor.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pun to make a serious point?
options: Elections happen every few years in many countries around the world.
Politicians work in government offices and meet with many different people.
Some politicians promise to raise standards, but only their own salaries rise.
People vote in schools, mosques and public halls on election day.
questions.why: Raise is used with two meanings for irony.

questions.stem: A store called "Curl Up & Dye" is a hair salon. What makes the name clever?
options: It names the owner of the salon and his family.
Dye sounds like die, and curl up has two meanings.
It rhymes with salon and sounds nice to say.
It is long and has many words in it, so people remember it.
questions.why: It plays on sound and meaning.

questions.stem: Why might puns be hard to translate into another language?
options: Puns are too short to be put into words in other languages.
The double meaning depends on words in one language.
Other languages have no jokes at all, so puns fail.
Puns use numbers, and numbers differ between languages.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a spoonerism (swapping sounds for wordplay)?
options: "Break a leg."
"It's raining cats and dogs."
"Time flies."
"You hissed my mystery lecture" for "You missed my history lecture."

questions.stem: A speaker says, "We need a crosswalk near school because many cars drive fast there." What is the reason?
options: many cars drive fast there
cars are loud on the road
school is big and old
we need a crosswalk there

questions.stem: Which is evidence a speaker could use to support "Our library needs more books"?
options: I like reading, and so do my friends and my teacher at school.
The library is quiet, and the chairs there are very soft and new.
Half the shelves are empty, and students wait weeks for popular books.
Books are nice, and they have bright covers with pictures on them.

questions.stem: What should a good listener do to find a speaker's main point?
options: look out the window and watch the people outside
count the speaker's words and write down how many there were
listen for what the speaker wants the audience to think or do
think about lunch and what you will eat after school
questions.why: The main point is the speaker's message.

questions.stem: A speaker says, "I think we should have a class pet. Pets teach responsibility." What is the claim?
options: Pets teach responsibility.
We should have a class pet.
I think.
Pets are animals.
questions.why: The claim is the speaker's position.

questions.stem: Which question helps you check a speaker's evidence?
options: Is the speaker tall?
What time is it?
What color is the speaker's shirt?
How does the speaker know this?
questions.why: Asking how they know checks evidence.

questions.stem: A speaker gives a reason but no facts. What is missing?
options: evidence
a speaker
a title
a claim

questions.stem: A speaker says, "Recycling helps. Last year our school recycled 2 tons of paper." What kind of evidence is this?
options: a joke
a personal opinion
a question
a statistic

questions.stem: Which reason is NOT relevant to "The school day should start later"?
options: Buses would face less traffic.
Students would get more sleep.
Tired students learn less.
The cafeteria has new tables.
questions.why: Tables do not relate to start times.

questions.stem: A speaker quotes a doctor about sleep. Why does this strengthen the speech?
options: Doctors are famous people.
An expert adds credibility.
It changes the topic of the talk.
Quotes are long and take time.

questions.stem: How can you tell whether a speaker's claim is supported?
options: Count the slides and see how many there are.
See if the speaker is loud and speaks quickly.
Check whether facts, examples or expert views back it up.
Check if the speech is long enough to fill the class time.

questions.stem: A speaker says, "Everyone agrees with me." What is the problem?
options: It is not evidence and may not be true.
It quotes an expert in the field of health.
It is too specific for a debate.
It is a statistic from a survey.

questions.stem: A speaker argues for a new park and says, "Studies show green spaces lower stress, and our town has none within two miles." Evaluate this support.
options: It combines research with a local fact, so it is strong.
It contains no evidence at all for its claim, so it is weak and not good.
It is irrelevant to the idea of a park, since it talks about stress only.
It is only an opinion that nobody can check, so it does not help the speaker.
questions.why: Research plus local data is strong support.

questions.stem: Which question best evaluates a speaker's statistic?
options: Do I like the number, and is it my lucky number?
Is the number odd or even, and is it small?
Where did the number come from, and is it recent?
Is the number big enough to fit on a slide?

questions.stem: A speaker uses a dramatic story about one student to argue a rule affects everyone. What is the weakness?
options: One example may not represent everyone.
It quotes an expert in the field of health.
Stories are always false and never true.
It uses statistics from a big survey.

questions.stem: Which response best summarizes how a speaker supported a claim?
options: She talked about recess and about how much fun it is for students.
She spoke for five minutes and then sat down before the end of the class period.
She was a good speaker and used a loud, clear voice in the hall.
She argued for longer recess using research on focus and teachers' observations.
questions.why: It names the claim and the evidence.

questions.stem: A speaker ignores a strong opposing argument. How does this affect the speech?
options: It has no effect on the speech or on the people who listen.
It adds more evidence to the speaker's own main claim.
It weakens credibility because listeners may doubt the claim.
It makes the speech stronger because it sounds sure.

questions.stem: In science, what does observe mean?
options: forget
watch carefully
guess
draw

questions.stem: In a math or science text, what is a measurement?
options: the size or amount of something found with a tool
a feeling that you have deep in your heart
a color that you can see on the wall
a story that your teacher tells you in the class

questions.stem: In social studies, a community is—
options: a math problem for the class to solve
a kind of animal that lives in groups
a type of weather that comes in winter
a group of people living in the same area

questions.stem: What does habitat mean in a science text?
options: a food that animals eat daily
a tool used for digging in gardens
the natural home of a plant or animal
a kind of habit that people have every day
questions.why: A habitat is a home in nature.

questions.stem: In "The liquid will evaporate in the sun," what does evaporate mean?
options: grow taller in the warm sun and in the rain
spill over the edge of a glass cup
freeze into ice in the cold night air
change into a gas and disappear into the air

questions.stem: In history, what is a timeline?
options: a map showing places in the town
a clock showing the hour of the day
a line showing events in order of time
a list showing names in a book

questions.stem: In "The colonists traded furs for tools," what does traded mean?
options: lost, so that it cannot be found
exchanged one thing for another
hid, so that nobody can see it
built, as a house is built

questions.stem: A science text says a material is a conductor. What does it do?
options: makes sound when it is turned on
stops all electricity from passing through
allows heat or electricity to pass through
changes color when it gets very hot

questions.stem: In "The region has a dry climate," what does climate mean?
options: today's temperature in the city at noon
a season of the year, like winter or summer
a mountain near the town and its streams
the usual weather of a place over a long time

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "Plants use sunlight to make food in a process called ____."
options: erosion
photosynthesis
migration
evaporation

questions.stem: In "The government passed a new law," what does government mean?
options: a school club that students join after class each week
the group that makes and enforces rules for a country
a business that sells things to people in the city
a family that lives together in one house with children

questions.stem: In "Erosion gradually reshaped the canyon," what does erosion mean?
options: the wearing away of land by water, wind or ice
the building of new rock under the sea
the growth of plants on the hills
a sudden earthquake in the mountains of Asia

questions.stem: In "The economy grew as exports increased," what are exports?
options: factories
goods bought from other countries
taxes
goods sent to other countries to sell

questions.stem: A science article says the results were "statistically significant." What does it most likely mean?
options: the results were wrong and had to be checked
the results are unlikely to be due to chance
the results were large numbers on the chart
the results were exciting for the scientists
questions.why: Significance means not likely by chance.

questions.stem: In "The treaty ended the conflict between the nations," what is a treaty?
options: a battle fought between two large armies
a border between two countries
a king who rules over two nations
a formal agreement between countries

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The cell's ____ controls its activities."
options: nucleus
orbit
atmosphere
membrane
questions.why: The nucleus is the control center.

questions.stem: Which word means to tell how two things are alike?
options: compare
count
repeat
describe

questions.stem: What does it mean to explain an answer?
options: guess what the answer is
tell why or how it is true
write it quickly on paper
erase it from the page

questions.stem: Which word means to put things in order from first to last?
options: predict
sequence
describe
measure

questions.stem: A test asks you to identify the main idea. What should you do?
options: find and name the main idea
skip it and go on to the next one
copy the whole text onto your paper
draw the main idea in a picture

questions.stem: What does summarize mean?
options: tell the most important parts briefly
add your own opinion only, not the facts
write a new story about the same topic
tell every detail, from start to end

questions.stem: Which word means a guess based on clues?
options: title
fact
prediction
label

questions.stem: A question asks you to justify your answer. What should you add?
options: nothing more than the answer itself
reasons or evidence that support it
a new question for your teacher
a drawing in your notebook

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The author uses facts to ____ her claim."
options: support
erase
hide
forget

questions.stem: What does it mean to analyze a poem?
options: read it once quickly and then stop
copy it word for word in your notebook
examine its parts closely to understand it
memorize it and say it out loud to the class

questions.stem: Which word means the effect something has?
options: symbol
detail
title
impact

questions.stem: In "The data reveal a pattern," what does reveal mean?
options: erase
show
question
hide

questions.stem: A prompt asks you to evaluate an argument. What should you do?
options: copy it word for word onto your page and hand it in
agree with the writer automatically, with no thinking
judge how strong and convincing it is, with reasons
list its words in a long list, one by one

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The two studies reached ____ conclusions, so scientists debated them."
options: brief
contradictory
simple
identical

questions.stem: In "The evidence is insufficient to prove the claim," what does insufficient mean?
options: too much
unrelated
not enough
very strong

questions.stem: What does it mean to synthesize information?
options: repeat a fact from one source again and again word by word
combine ideas from several sources into one understanding
copy one source word for word onto your own paper
delete sources and throw away the pages you do not like

questions.stem: Which word best describes a claim based on careful reasoning?
options: emotional
unclear
random
logical

the cook
nobody
the cake

The letter was written by Sam.
Sam writes letters to Ali.
Sam will write a letter.

options: The choir was sung.
Sung was the song.
The choir sang the song.
The song sang the choir.

questions.stem: What is a sign of passive voice?
options: a plural noun at the end of every sentence
a question mark at the end of the sentence
a form of be plus a past participle, often with by
an adjective before every noun in the sentence

questions.stem: Which sentence names the doer first?
options: Chased was the cat.
The dog chased the cat.
The cat was chased.
The cat was chased by the dog.
questions.why: Active voice puts the doer first.

questions.stem: Rewrite in passive voice: "The wind knocked down the fence."
options: Knocked down the fence by the wind.
The wind was knocked down by the fence.
The fence knocked the wind down hard.
The fence was knocked down by the wind.

questions.stem: Which sentence is clearer and more direct?
options: A trophy winning happened.
The trophy was won.
The team won the trophy.
The trophy was won by the team.

questions.stem: When is passive voice a good choice?
options: when the doer is unknown or unimportant
only in poems and in songs written long ago
always, in every kind of writing
never, because it is always wrong

questions.stem: Which sentence uses passive voice without naming the doer?
options: The principal changed the rules.
The rules were changed last week.
We changed the rules.
They change rules.

options: neither
active
passive
both

questions.stem: A news report says, "Errors were made in the counting." Why might the writer choose passive voice?

to show that this will happen in the future
to add detail about the people in the story
to make the sentence longer for the reader

questions.stem: Which revision fixes an awkward shift in voice? "Rami painted the fence, and then the gate was painted by him."
options: The fence was painted, and Rami painted.
Rami painted, and the gate painted.
The gate and fence were by Rami.
Rami painted the fence and then the gate.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses passive voice appropriately in a science report?
options: We are heating samples now, maybe.
Samples heat themselves.
The samples were heated for ten minutes.
I heated the samples because I wanted to.
questions.why: Science reports focus on the procedure.

questions.stem: Change to active voice: "The proposal has been rejected by the committee."
options: The committee was rejected.
The committee has rejected the proposal.
The proposal has rejected the committee.
Rejected the proposal has.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

The documents are being reviewed by lawyers.
Lawyers are reviewing the documents now.
Lawyers review documents every single day.

questions.stem: The root photo means light. What does a photograph capture?
options: a taste of sweet things
a smell from the garden
a sound made by a bell
an image made with light

questions.stem: The root micro means small. What does a microscope help you see?
options: big buildings
very small things
loud sounds
faraway stars

questions.stem: The root therm means heat. What does a thermometer measure?
options: weight
temperature
speed
distance

questions.stem: The root geo means earth. What does geography study?
options: animals only and their food
the earth and its features
numbers and how to add them
music and the words of songs

questions.stem: The root phon means sound. Which word is about sound?
options: photograph
microphone
biology
geology

questions.stem: The root auto means self. What is an autobiography?
options: a life story written by the person themselves
a science report about plants and animals
a story about cars and the people who drive them
a car manual for fixing old engines
questions.why: Auto = self, bio = life, graph = write.

questions.stem: The root spect means look. What does a spectator do?
options: sells tickets
plays the game
watches an event
cleans the stadium

questions.stem: The root rupt means break. What happens when a volcano erupts?
options: it bursts or breaks out
it grows taller slowly
it sleeps
it freezes

questions.stem: The root mal means bad. What is a malfunction?
options: a happy event at a party or a wedding
a new machine in a factory or a shop
a failure to work correctly
a fast car on the road to town

questions.stem: The root cred means believe. What does credible mean?
options: colorful
unbelievable
loud
believable

questions.stem: The roots tele (far) and vis (see) form television. What does it do?
options: measures heat from a big fire
shows pictures sent from far away
plays only music for the family
writes letters to the people

questions.stem: The root ject means throw. What does reject mean?
options: hide something away
accept it happily
throw back or refuse
build it up again

questions.stem: Using roots, what does circumnavigate mean? (circum = around, nav = ship/sail)

questions.why: Plays use asides, soliloquies or acting.

questions.stem: A play version leaves out a minor character from the book. Why might the director do this?

to keep the performance shorter and focused
to add more pages and make the play longer
to confuse the audience on purpose at the end

questions.stem: Which detail in a performance could change how the audience feels about a scene?
options: the ticket price at the door of the hall
the program's paper color and its size
dramatic music during a quiet moment
the theater's address on the street

questions.stem: The stage directions say "(sadly)." How might an actor show this?
options: by speaking softly and looking down
by singing a happy song out loud
by running offstage with a big smile
by laughing loudly at the other actors

questions.stem: What is one advantage of reading a story rather than watching a play?
options: you can imagine details yourself and reread
you see costumes and sets on a stage in a hall
you hear music and singing in a hall at night
you see real actors in the theater up close

questions.stem: A film version adds a scene not in the story. How should a reader evaluate this change?

assume the film is always better than the book it comes from
decide whether it supports or changes the story's message
assume it is a mistake made by the director

questions.stem: A director stages a story in a modern city instead of a village. What effect might this have?

it makes the story silent, with no one speaking
it makes the old story feel relevant to today
it changes nothing about the story at all

questions.stem: How can an actor's interpretation make a character more sympathetic than in the text?
options: by standing still and saying nothing at all on the whole stage
by wearing bright colors that match the stage lights
by saying fewer lines than the other actors do
through gentle tone and expressions that show hidden feelings

questions.stem: Which question best compares a story to its performance?
options: How did the performance's choices change my understanding of the main character?

What snacks were sold, and how much did they cost at the theater?
How long was the show, and when did it begin in the evening?

questions.stem: Why might a performance cut a character's long inner monologue?
options: inner thoughts are harder to show on stage, so action replaces them
it makes the play longer than it needs to be for the crowd that watches it
monologues are not allowed in any play at all in a school or a theater
the actor forgot it on the day of the show at the theater, so it was cut

the author's name
the setting
the page numbers

the time of year
the characters
the titles

to choose a favorite cover for the books
to count the words in each of the stories

the same way in both of the stories
they don't travel in either story
by horse in A and by car in B

questions.stem: Which word helps compare two settings?

suddenly
because
both

both are in space, far away from the Earth

both have weather that changes during the year

readers cannot tell the difference between them
only titles matter, not the details inside
each author chooses different details and moods

questions.stem: Two stories describe the same forest. One calls it "whispering and welcoming," the other "dark and tangled." What differs?

the forest's location on a map
the mood each author creates
the season and the weather

questions.stem: What is the best way to organize a comparison of two settings?

a map of your school and the yard around it
a Venn diagram showing similarities and differences
a list of characters only, with no places at all

questions.stem: Story A's crowded city makes the hero feel lonely; Story B's empty desert makes the hero feel free. What does this comparison show?

settings do not matter at all to how characters feel
setting can shape characters' feelings in opposite ways
cities are always better than deserts for living

how each location changed what people experienced
the publication price of each book in the shop
the font size of each text and its title

One story is longer than the other by many pages, and it has more chapters in it too.
questions.why: It compares purpose, not just presence.

to add more characters and a busy town

islands are always warm and have lots of food

questions.stem: A reader notices both stories end at sunrise. What might this shared detail symbolize?

the stories are boring
it is breakfast time
the characters are tired

a kind of food that people eat at lunch
a way of seeing or thinking about something

generosity
anger
fear

options: to understand and respect different people
to skip pages that are too hard to read

to make reading harder for children

"I'd love to learn how your family celebrates."

how to build a school of brick and stone and glass

culture affects only the clothes people wear and the food they eat
everyone notices the same things in any place, so background has no role

Where was the book printed, and by which company, and in which year?

stories are always false and made up by writers
it is too long for most readers to finish

Both texts have titles at the top of the page, and both have a few nice pictures too.
I liked both texts, and I read them twice, because they were both so much fun to read, I think.
Both authors show courage: Lina speaks up in Text 1, while Sami protects his sister in Text 2.

questions.stem: Why should writers avoid 'dropping' a quote without explanation?
options: readers may not see how it supports the point
explanations are boring for most readers
quotes are not allowed in school essays
it makes writing shorter and easier to read

questions.stem: Which is the strongest analysis of evidence?
options: There are doors in the story, and there are windows too, in the old house of the family, so it is a common thing.
The repeated image of locked doors suggests the character feels trapped by her family's expectations.
The story mentions doors three times in the first two pages of it, and that is all that the writer says of them.
Doors are locked at night, so the family is safe in the house, and the writer wants us to see this.

questions.stem: "My brother got a cold after eating ice cream, so ice cream causes colds." What is wrong?
options: one event happening after another does not prove cause
it quotes an expert who knows about food and health
it uses too many facts to prove the idea is true
it is a fair argument that most people will accept

questions.stem: "Everyone has this toy, so you should buy it too." What kind of reasoning is this?
options: expert evidence from a scientist
bandwagon (following the crowd)
a statistic from a big study
a fair comparison of two toys

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to eat vegetables?
options: Some vegetables are long and thin like a stick or a pen.
Vegetables contain vitamins that help the body grow.
My friend eats them at lunch every day, so I should too.
Vegetables are green, red, and orange in color, and they are nice.

questions.stem: What makes an argument strong?
options: repeating the claim again and again
loud words and a shouting voice
insults against the other side
clear reasons supported by evidence

questions.stem: "You can't trust Ali's idea about recycling because he is messy." What is wrong?
options: it is fair to judge him by his room
it is a fact that people can check
it attacks the person, not the idea
it uses evidence from his work at home

questions.stem: Which question helps check an argument?
options: Is the paper white and clean enough to use?
Is it Monday or Tuesday on the calendar today?
Is there evidence for this claim?
Is the speaker tall enough to be seen by all?

questions.stem: "Either we cancel the trip, or everyone will get lost." What is the flaw?
options: it quotes an expert from a famous university
it uses a statistic from a very small and old survey
it offers only two options when there are others
it is too long and has too many examples

questions.stem: "Three students said the cafeteria food is bad, so all students hate it." What is the flaw?
options: it is an expert opinion from a trusted teacher
it uses too many examples from the whole school
it generalizes from too few examples
it is a fact that was checked by the cook

questions.stem: Which evidence is most relevant to "Our town needs more bike lanes"?
options: Bike lanes are painted green on the road in the city center.
My uncle owns a car, and it is red, and it is fast.
Bikes come in many colors and sizes, and in many prices.
Bike accidents rose 20% last year on roads without lanes.

questions.stem: "If we let students use phones at lunch, soon they'll use them all day and never learn." What is the flaw?
options: it gives a counterargument and answers it with a fair reason, so it is strong
it uses data from a study to prove its point to readers
it is balanced and fair to both sides of the question
it assumes one small step leads to extreme results (slippery slope)

questions.stem: An ad says a famous singer uses a toothpaste. Why is this weak evidence?
options: it is too scientific for most people to understand
it is a statistic from a large and fair study
singers never brush their teeth in the morning
a singer is not an expert on dental health

questions.stem: "Since the new principal arrived, test scores fell. She must be a bad leader." Which question best exposes the flaw?
options: When did she arrive at the school, and from where?
How tall is the principal, and how old is she?
What other causes could explain the drop?
What is her name, and where does she live?

questions.stem: Which argument uses circular reasoning?
options: Readers rated it 4.8 out of 5 stars on the web, so it is good.
Teachers recommend it for its themes and ideas, and for its words.
This book won three awards from librarians in town, so it is good.
This book is the best because it is better than all the others.
questions.why: It restates the claim as proof.

questions.stem: A writer cites a study funded by a candy company showing candy is healthy. What should a reader consider?
options: that the study is too short to read
that candy is sweet and children like it
nothing; studies are always fair and true
possible bias from the funding source

questions.stem: Which response best evaluates an argument?
options: The claim is supported by recent data, but the writer ignores the cost concern raised by opponents.
It is long, and it has many paragraphs and a lot of words in each one of them.
I agree with the writer because I like the topic and I like the way it sounds.
The writer uses words, sentences and paragraphs to tell the readers about the topic of the essay.

questions.stem: "Scientists don't know everything about the ocean, so my theory about sea monsters must be true." What flaw is this?
options: using reliable evidence from many trusted science books and sea experts
a fair comparison between two things that are alike
arguing that a lack of proof against something proves it
a strong statistic from a large study of the sea

How long do elephants live?

questions.why: It can be answered with facts.

How hot is the sun?
questions.why: Everything about space is too broad.

How do volcanoes form deep inside the earth?
questions.why: It has no sources and no depth.

How
Do
Can

questions.stem: Which research question fits a report on clean energy?
options: What is my favorite color of the sun and the sky?
How do solar panels turn sunlight into electricity?
Do I like the sun when it is hot outside?
Is energy good or bad for people everywhere?

questions.stem: Why are yes/no questions weak research questions?
options: they can be answered without explanation or evidence
they are too long to read in one go, so they bore readers
they need many sources to be answered well
they are always false and cannot be proven by anyone

What will the weather be in 3025?
What is my teacher thinking?

questions.stem: Which question is best for a multi-source research paper?
options: Are phones fun to play with at home or at school or in the car?
What is a phone and who made the first one in the world, long ago?
Do teenagers have phones in their pockets at school and at home?
How have smartphones changed the way teenagers communicate since 2010?

"Video games?"

questions.stem: What makes a research question 'arguable' enough for an essay?

it is about the writer's feelings and his mood on the day he writes
reasonable people could reach different conclusions from evidence

How has rising sea level affected coastal cities in the last 30 years?
Is the weather changing in the whole world this year?
questions.why: Place, effect and time narrow it.

questions.stem: Why might a researcher refine a question after initial reading?
