questions.stem: What is historical fiction?
options: a true biography of a famous man or woman
a made-up story set in a real time in the past
a science report about the world and space
a poem about the future of the Earth and stars
questions.why: It mixes invented stories with real history.

questions.stem: In a historical fiction story about ancient Egypt, which detail is likely real history?
options: a talking cat that solves crimes
the main character's best friend
pyramids being built along the Nile
the hero's secret diary

questions.stem: Why do authors write historical fiction?
options: to describe the future of cities and robots
to help readers imagine life in the past
to teach math to children in the class
to report today's news about sports and weather

questions.stem: Which source would help check if a historical fiction detail is true?
options: a history book or encyclopedia
another novel about the same time
a joke book for young children
a cartoon on television at night

questions.stem: A story says characters traveled by train in 1700. What is the problem?
options: trains did not exist then
nothing is wrong at all
trains are slow and loud
1700 is a good year for it

questions.stem: Which character is most likely invented in a historical novel?
options: the real king who ruled the land
a farm girl who meets a real king
the real queen of the old kingdom
a real general who led the army
questions.why: Ordinary main characters are often invented.

questions.stem: How is historical fiction different from a history textbook?
options: it has no facts at all, only made-up stories
it adds invented characters, dialogue and feelings
it is always shorter than a school history textbook
it has charts and maps in every chapter

questions.stem: A novel describes a real battle but adds a boy messenger. How should readers think about the boy?
options: he was the general of the whole army in the battle and its leader
he is the author of the book himself, in disguise as a boy
he is likely invented to show the event from a personal view
he must be real, since the book says so on the page

questions.stem: Why might an author change small historical details?
options: to make the story flow, often explained in an author's note
because history is unknown and nobody wrote anything down
to make it longer by adding many more pages and names
to trick readers into believing a false history

questions.stem: What is an author's note in historical fiction usually for?
options: to name the publisher and the printing house
to explain what is true and what is invented
to give the price of the book in the shop
to list the chapters and their page numbers

questions.stem: Comparing a novel's battle scene to a history book, a reader notices different dates. What should they conclude?
options: both are correct, so you can trust all the dates in each one
history books are always wrong, so trust the novel instead
the novel may have changed facts; trust reliable history sources
dates don't matter, so a reader can ignore the difference

questions.stem: Why might an author portray a real historical figure in a way that differs from historians' accounts?
options: to make the book shorter for young readers
by accident always, with no idea in mind
because historians are always wrong about the past
to explore a theme or offer a new interpretation

questions.stem: Which question best compares a fictional and historical portrayal of an event?
options: How does the novel's focus on one family change our understanding of the event?
Which book is longer, the novel or the history book that we read?
Which cover is nicer, the one with the boy on it or the one with the ship?
Who printed the books, and in which city were they first sold?

questions.stem: A historical novel shows ordinary people's struggles, while a textbook lists dates and leaders. What does the novel add?
options: nothing new about the people of the time
emotional, human understanding of the period
more accurate dates than the textbook gives
a list of leaders and their long names

questions.stem: What is a responsible way for a historical novelist to handle real events?
options: ignore history and write a new story
change everything about the events
research carefully and note any changes
copy a textbook word for word

questions.stem: A reader finds a historical novel's portrayal of a culture stereotyped. What should the reader do?
options: accept it as fact because it is printed in a book
ignore all history and read only today's news from the web
stop reading all books about the past and about other lands
compare with reliable sources and voices from that culture

questions.stem: What is a firsthand account?
options: told by someone who was there
a poem
a made-up story
told by someone who read about it later
questions.why: Firsthand means the writer experienced it.

questions.stem: Which word often shows a firsthand account?
options: people
I
scientists
they
questions.why: First-person pronouns show the writer was there.

questions.stem: Which is a secondhand account?
options: a diary entry written during the flood
an encyclopedia article about a flood
a photo taken by a witness
a letter from a flood survivor
questions.why: Encyclopedias are written by people who weren't there.

questions.stem: A boy writes, "I saw the eclipse from my roof." What kind of account is this?
options: firsthand
fiction
secondhand
an opinion poll

questions.stem: Which source is firsthand?
options: a news summary written years later
an astronaut's journal from space
a textbook chapter about space
a website for kids about planets

questions.stem: What is a secondhand account?
options: told by the person who lived it and saw everything happen
a song lyric that a singer wrote about love
a list of words with their meanings in a book
told by someone who learned about the event from others

questions.stem: What does a firsthand account usually include that a secondhand one may not?
options: personal feelings and sensory details
many statistics from different places
an index
a list of sources

questions.stem: What does a secondhand account often include that a firsthand one may not?
options: only one person's view
a diary date
background facts and several viewpoints
the writer's feelings in the moment

questions.stem: A reporter interviews a firefighter and writes an article. The firefighter's quotes are—
options: an opinion poll about the fire in town and its causes
fiction written by the reporter himself for the paper
firsthand information inside a secondhand account
a secondhand rumor from a neighbor of the firefighter
questions.why: The quotes come from a witness.

questions.stem: Why might two accounts of the same storm differ?
options: they use different fonts and colours on the page of the book
one writer is always lying to the readers of the story
storms happen twice in the same week in that town
one is personal and emotional; the other is factual and general

questions.stem: Which detail most likely comes from a firsthand account?
options: "The storm caused $2 million in damage."
"Experts say storms are increasing."
"My hands shook as the water rose past my knees."
"The region has many rivers."

questions.stem: A historian uses a soldier's letters to write a book. Why are the letters valuable?
options: they are always fully accurate and never biased
they include statistics about the whole army
they are written many years later by other people
they give direct evidence of the soldier's experience

questions.stem: What is a limitation of firsthand accounts?
options: they are too general to help the reader at all
they are always invented by the person who writes
they show only one person's view and may be biased
they never include details about the event or place

questions.stem: Which question best compares a firsthand and a secondhand account of the same event?
options: Who printed it, and in which year was the book first printed in the city?
Which one has more pages in all, and how many pages does each one have?
How does each account's focus change what readers understand about the event?
Which cover is nicer to look at, and which colours does it use on the front?

questions.stem: A secondhand account quotes three witnesses who disagree. What should a careful reader conclude?
options: the event did not happen at all, and the witnesses made it up
only the first witness matters, so ignore the rest
the event may be interpreted differently; compare the evidence
all witnesses are lying about it, so trust nobody

questions.stem: Why might a secondhand account be more reliable for numbers like casualties?
options: witnesses always lie when they talk about what they saw
it is written faster than a first account is, by the writer
the writer can gather data from many official sources afterward
it has more feelings in it than a first account does have
questions.why: Later research can be more complete.

questions.stem: What is a flashback?
options: the story's title that is written at the top of the cover
the ending of the story, where the problem is solved
a scene that goes back to something that happened earlier
a hint about the future that comes later in the story

questions.stem: "Years ago, when Tariq was five, he lost his dog." What is this?
options: a setting
foreshadowing
a flashback
a summary

questions.stem: Which words often signal a flashback?
options: "Next week..."
"Suddenly..."
"She remembered when..."
"In conclusion..."

questions.stem: What is foreshadowing?
options: a conclusion at the end of a story
a memory from the past of a character
a clue about what will happen later
a character list at the front of a play

questions.stem: Why might an author use a flashback?
options: to describe the cover and the title page
to explain why a character acts a certain way
to end the story in a happy way for everyone
to name the characters at the start of the story

questions.stem: A story mentions an old map hidden in the attic early on. What might this foreshadow?
options: a birthday party for the girl who lives there
a math lesson in the school next door
nothing about the story at all, in fact
a treasure hunt or discovery later
questions.why: Early details hint at later events.

questions.stem: How is a flashback different from foreshadowing?
options: flashbacks only happen in poems and in songs, never in novels
a flashback shows the past; foreshadowing hints at the future
they are the same thing in a story or a film
foreshadowing shows the past of the hero in a story
questions.why: They move in opposite directions in time.

questions.stem: A character flinches when she hears thunder, then remembers a storm that destroyed her home. What does the flashback reveal?
options: the cause of her fear
the ending
the weather forecast
her favorite color

questions.stem: Which sentence foreshadows danger?
options: Nobody noticed the rope was beginning to fray.
They bought rope for the boat at the shop in town.
The rope was long and strong, and it was new.
Rope is useful for many jobs on a boat or a farm.
questions.why: A fraying rope hints at trouble.

questions.stem: How do authors signal the end of a flashback?
options: by returning to present-tense events or a time phrase like "Now,"
they never do, and readers have to guess it without any help
by ending the book soon after the memory finishes
by changing the font only, to make the letters bigger

questions.stem: What effect does foreshadowing have on readers?
options: it confuses them forever, even at the end
it removes interest in the rest of the story
it builds suspense and makes them predict
it lists facts about the characters

questions.stem: A story opens with the hero in prison, then flashes back to show how he got there. What is the effect?
options: it changes the genre of the story completely, from a tale to a poem
it spoils nothing about the ending, so the reader is not curious
it removes suspense entirely from the plot and the setting
it creates curiosity about how events led to this point

questions.stem: Which is the best example of subtle foreshadowing?
options: Passengers boarded the ship in a long line, one by one, with their bags and hats.
A storm is coming, the captain announced to all the people on the ship at noon.
It was a ship, and it was big and white and new, with a tall red flag.
The captain glanced twice at the barometer before smiling at the passengers.
questions.why: A small detail hints without telling.

questions.stem: How can a flashback deepen a theme of forgiveness?
options: by listing the setting of the story in great detail
by ending the story early, long before the problem begins
by describing the weather on the day of the event itself
by showing the past wrong that a character must now forgive

questions.stem: Why might an author combine flashback and foreshadowing in one chapter?
options: to make the chapter shorter
to remove characters
to connect past causes with future consequences
to confuse time on purpose without meaning
questions.why: Linking past and future builds structure.

questions.stem: A memory a character mentions in chapter 1 becomes important in chapter 10. In chapter 1, the memory served as—
options: a title
foreshadowing
a resolution
a climax

read all the steps before starting
start with the last step and go back
guess what to do and begin to work

first
because
but

color it with a red crayon
fold it so the two sides meet
crumple it into a ball and throw it

questions.stem: In a recipe, what does "step 3" mean?

the third thing to do
three people cook at once
use three eggs in the cake

questions.stem: Why are numbered steps helpful?
options: they show the exact order
they make the text longer
they show prices
they are decorations

questions.stem: What should you do if a step is unclear?
options: stop forever and never try again
reread it or look at the diagram
do the opposite of what it says
skip all steps and begin at the end

eating
baking
buying flour

to list prices of the things you buy
so you gather everything before starting
to make the page look full of words

questions.stem: Directions say, "Wait until the glue is dry before painting." What happens if you skip the wait?
options: the glue disappears and the wood is clean
it dries faster when you paint over the top
the paint may smear and the project may fail
nothing changes, and the project looks the same

questions.stem: Which detail in directions is a warning?
options: Caution: the pan will be hot.
Mix well before you put it in the oven.
Serves four people at the table.
Add salt to taste after you cook it.

questions.stem: What text feature helps most with following assembly directions?
options: labeled diagrams
the author's biography
a long introduction
a poem

questions.stem: A procedure has steps 1–6, but step 4 says, "Repeat steps 2 and 3 three times." How many times will you do step 2 in total?

six
four
two

questions.stem: Why might a technical manual include troubleshooting steps at the end?
options: to help when something does not work as expected
to add jokes for the readers to enjoy and to laugh at
to list prices of the parts and the tools in a shop
to describe the long history of the product and its maker

questions.stem: Which revision makes a direction clearer? "Put it in the thing."
options: Put the thing in it, please, and then shut it tight.
Insert the thing in the place where it fits the best.
Place the battery in the slot on the back of the remote.
Put it in the place that you like the most today.

questions.stem: A lab procedure says to measure 25 mL, but you measure 2.5 mL. What is the most likely result?
options: nothing changes in the experiment at all
the experiment's results will be inaccurate
it doubles the result of the experiment
it will work better than before, as expected

questions.stem: Why do procedures often use command verbs like "stir" and "pour"?
options: they ask questions to the people who read them
they are polite and sound friendly to readers
they tell readers exactly what action to take

they are the same kind of story in every way
fantasy is always true and based on real events

science fiction
poetry

it is always true and has no made-up parts

drama and recipe in one story together
realistic fiction and fantasy (magical realism)

sets.skill: How Authors Develop and Refine Ideas

questions.stem: How does an author usually introduce a main idea?
options: only in the last word of the whole text
in the title only, on the cover
never, because it is not needed
in a topic sentence near the beginning

questions.stem: What do supporting details do?
options: list the author's friends and family
change the topic of the text
tell jokes to make readers laugh
explain and prove the main idea

questions.stem: Which detail supports "Dogs make helpful pets"?
options: Dogs have tails, ears, and four legs.
Some dogs guide people who cannot see.
Dogs bark loudly at strangers at night.
Dogs come in many colors and sizes.

questions.stem: Why do authors give examples?
options: to end the text
to fill space
to make ideas clear
to confuse readers

questions.stem: What does the conclusion of an informational text usually do?
options: start a new topic
sum up the main idea
list random facts
ask the reader to stop

questions.stem: Which sentence adds more detail to "Bees are important"?
options: Bees buzz loudly around the flowers in the garden.
Bees are yellow and black in color.
I saw a bee in the garden today.
Bees pollinate many of the fruits we eat.

questions.stem: How does an author refine an idea across paragraphs?
options: each paragraph repeats the same sentence word for word
by changing topics randomly in every paragraph
by removing details from each paragraph
each paragraph adds new evidence or a new angle
questions.why: Ideas grow as the text continues.

questions.stem: An article first says "Recycling helps," then shows how it saves energy, then how it reduces landfills. What is the author doing?
options: contradicting the idea in the first line
developing the idea with specific reasons
listing unrelated facts about other topics
telling a story about a recycling truck

questions.stem: Which transition shows an author is adding a new point?
options: In contrast,
Although
Furthermore,
However,

questions.stem: Why might an author include a quote from an expert in the middle of an article?
options: to end the article with a final word
to strengthen the idea with credible support
to change the subject to something new and different
to add humor so that readers laugh

questions.stem: How does a strong final paragraph connect to the introduction?
options: it returns to the main idea with new understanding
it repeats the first sentence exactly, word for word
it lists sources only, without any ideas
it introduces a new topic that is not related

questions.stem: An essay begins with a broad claim, then narrows to one city's example. What is the purpose?
options: to show the claim in a concrete, convincing case
to avoid evidence in the whole essay and the claim
to confuse readers about the main claim for fun
to change the claim in the last part of it

questions.stem: How can an author's use of a counterexample refine an idea?
options: it removes evidence so the claim looks stronger
it adds humor so that readers enjoy the essay more
it shows the limits of the claim, making it more precise
it proves the claim wrong always, in every situation

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the author refining (qualifying) a claim?
options: Screen time can harm sleep, especially when used within an hour of bedtime.
Screens are bad for everyone, and nobody should ever use them.
Screens are good for everyone, and all people should use them more every day.
Everyone uses screens at home, at school and at work every day.

questions.stem: In a speech, an idea is repeated with growing intensity each time. What does this develop?
options: a counterargument for the other side
emphasis and emotional force
a new topic for the next speech
a list of facts about the idea

questions.stem: How do section headings help an author develop a complex idea?
options: they replace the text, so readers do not have to read the sections
they organize the idea into clear parts that build on each other
they decorate the page with color and big letters
they are only used for making the index at the back

fortytwo

forty-two

words left out or a pause
the end of a list of things

questions.stem: Which word is hyphenated correctly?

s-elfconfident
self-confident
self confident-

questions.stem: Which punctuation mark is longer than a hyphen and shows a break in thought?

a comma
a period
an apostrophe

questions.stem: Which sentence shows a pause with an ellipsis?

"Well, I'm not sure!"
"Well; I'm not sure."

My favorite fruit—mango—is in season.

questions.stem: Which is correctly hyphenated before a noun?
options: a wellwritten report
a-well-written report
a well written-report
a well-written report

options: She is a part-time worker.
He gave a last-minute speech.
It was a well-written report.
The report was well written.

"The... ship... sank."

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a dash to add emphasis?

She had one goal; victory.
She had one goal: victory?
She had one goal—victory.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a pair of dashes?

The old bridge—once the longest in the region was finally repaired.
The—old bridge once the longest was repaired.

questions.stem: Which compound modifier is hyphenated correctly?
options: a high quality-product
a high-quality-product
a high-quality product
a highly-qualified product

questions.stem: Why should writers avoid changing meaning when using an ellipsis in a quotation?
options: ellipses are not allowed in any school essay

it adds new words to the end of the quote
it would misrepresent the original author

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a hyphen to avoid confusion?
options: The team will recovers the chairs.
The team will re cover the chairs.
The team will re-cover the chairs with new fabric.
The team will recover the chairs with new fabric.

questions.stem: What is an inference?

a question with no answer at all
a fact copied from the text word for word
a smart guess using clues and what you know

questions.stem: The text says, "Mia's dog wagged its tail at the door." What can you infer?

the dog is lost in the street

questions.stem: A picture shows bare trees and children in coats. What season is it probably?
options: summer
spring
winter
it is impossible to know

options: the cat ate the food
the plate is new today
no one was hungry at home
the cat is scared of food
questions.why: The clues point to the cat.

questions.stem: How do illustrations help readers make inferences?
options: they show details like expressions and settings the text may not state
they replace all the words in the text with colors and shapes
they list the facts in the story in a table or a chart on the page
they give the page number of the scene to the reader of it, too

questions.stem: The text says, "Grandpa's hands shook as he opened the old letter." Which inference is best supported?

the letter is new and was sent today

options: a bright sun shining in the clear morning sky
boxes stacked by the door and empty shelves
a dog sleeping on the sofa all day
a bowl of fruit on the kitchen table

questions.stem: Text: "Omar said he was fine." Picture: Omar sits alone, head down, while others play. What is the best inference?
options: Omar is the game's leader and he is in charge
Omar is very happy to play by himself today
Omar is asleep on the ground after the game
Omar is not really fine; he feels left out

questions.stem: Why should readers use both the text and the picture when making inferences?
options: together they give more evidence than either alone
it is faster, so you finish the page sooner
text is always more correct than the picture
pictures are always more correct than the words

questions.stem: A picture book shows a character's shadow growing larger as she walks toward a stage. What might the illustrator suggest?
options: she is getting much taller
the stage lights are broken
it is getting dark outside
her confidence is growing

questions.stem: Which inference is NOT supported? Text: "The crowd went silent as the runner fell."
options: the crowd was surprised by the fall of the runner on the track
people were worried about the runner who had fallen to the ground
the fall was unexpected for everyone who sat in the stands
the crowd was cheering for another runner the whole time

questions.stem: An illustration shows a character in bright colors while everyone else is gray. What can you infer?
options: the printer was broken on that day, so the page has no color
it is a cartoon about paint and brushes for children
the character stands out or feels different from others

questions.stem: Which medium is best for comparing average rainfall in five cities?
options: a poem
a podcast
a bar graph

questions.stem: A news website shows an interactive map of earthquakes. How does interactivity help?
options: it replaces the article title with a map
it plays music while users read the map

questions.stem: A documentary and a textbook give different numbers about the same event. What should a reader do?
options: average the numbers from the two sources
check the sources and dates each one used

questions.stem: Why might a speech be more persuasive when watched than when read?
options: the words change when you watch it live

questions.stem: Which combination of media would best help someone learn to tie a knot?
options: step-by-step photos with a short video
a long paragraph only, with no pictures

a poem about ropes and the sea

questions.stem: How can an infographic mislead?

by citing sources at the bottom of the page

questions.stem: Why read two texts about the same topic?

to find the shortest one
to read less
to choose a favorite cover

options: Lions live in prides in the grasslands.
Lions roar at night in the grass.
Lions eat meat from big animals.
Lions are big cats with strong legs.

options: one text copied the other one badly
dolphins are fish that swim in the sea
the fact is probably reliable
the fact is wrong and not true

questions.stem: What should you do if two texts disagree?
options: make up an answer to it
check a third reliable source
ignore both of the texts
pick the longer text of the two

a timeline of your day
a word search
a calendar

questions.stem: Text 1 explains how rain forms. Text 2 explains floods. How do they connect?
options: heavy rain can cause floods
rain stops floods from coming
floods make clouds in the sky
they don't connect in any way

questions.stem: Which is the best summary that integrates two texts about the pyramids?
options: The pyramids are old and very big, and many tourists from all over the world visit them each year.
The pyramids were tombs built by thousands of workers using ramps and sledges.
I like Egypt because it has many old and interesting places.
Text 1 is long and Text 2 is short, so they are very different.
questions.why: It joins key facts from both.

questions.stem: Text 1 is a firsthand diary; Text 2 is a history article. How can a writer use both?
options: use only the article and leave out every personal detail of the people
use the diary for personal details and the article for facts and context
use neither one, and write only from what you remember
use only the diary and leave out all the historical facts

questions.stem: When writing about two texts, what should you include?
options: information from both, with credit to each
only the first text, because it is longer
only your opinion, with no facts from either text
the page numbers only, without any ideas

questions.stem: Text 1 says a law helped workers; Text 2 says it hurt small businesses. How should a report present this?
options: only the positive effect on workers
only the negative effect on shops
skip the law and talk about work
show both effects of the law

questions.stem: Text 1 gives data that plastic waste is rising; Text 2 describes a town that cut waste by 40%. What conclusion integrates both?
options: Towns are small and have few people in them, so nothing can be done to fix the waste.
Plastic waste is a growing problem, but local action can reduce it significantly.
Plastic is good for the earth, and it should be used more by every town and every school.

questions.stem: Why is integrating information more than listing facts from each text?

it removes facts from each of the texts it reads in class
it connects ideas to build a new, fuller understanding

questions.stem: Two scientists' articles disagree about a cause. What is the strongest way to integrate them?

questions.stem: A fire station burns down. What kind of irony is this?

a fact
a rhyme

a metaphor
verbal irony

a setting
a simile
verbal irony

tickets are made of paper and ink, not of metal

Dad fixed the tire in the garage on Sunday afternoon.

situational
verbal
dramatic

questions.stem: Why do authors use dramatic irony?
options: to name characters at the beginning of the story
to explain facts to the readers in a very clear and simple way
to build suspense because readers know what characters don't
to end the story with a surprise for the reader

questions.stem: A character says, "I'm never wrong," right before making a big mistake. What does this create?
options: irony
a summary
a flashback
a setting

questions.stem: Which is NOT an example of irony?
options: A chef cooks dinner for his family.

A spelling champion misspells his own name.
A lifeguard can't swim.

they feel worry as they watch the hero act on a lie
they feel nothing at all about the hero

a shorter play because the story ends sooner

questions.stem: What is the conflict in a story?
options: the setting where the story takes place
the title written on the front cover
the main problem the characters face
the author who wrote the whole story

questions.stem: What is the climax?
options: the cover of the book we read
the first page of the story it is in
the list of characters in the play
the most exciting turning point
questions.why: The climax is the high point.

questions.stem: What is the resolution?
options: the beginning of the story and its start
the setting of the story and its place
how the problem is solved at the end
the title of the story and its author

questions.stem: A boy loses his dog and searches for it. What is the conflict?
options: the boy's name
the color of the dog
the town
finding the lost dog

questions.stem: Which part of the plot comes first?
options: the resolution
the falling action
the climax
the introduction (exposition)

questions.stem: In a story, the girl finally finds her lost necklace. This is the—
options: conflict
introduction
resolution
setting

questions.stem: What is rising action?
options: the solution to the story's problem at the end
the title of the story or the book on the cover
events that build tension toward the climax
the last sentence of the story, at the end

questions.stem: Which is an example of internal conflict?
options: a storm hitting a town near the sea
a dog chasing a cat across the yard
two teams playing a game in the school park
a girl deciding whether to tell the truth

questions.stem: Which is an example of character vs. nature conflict?
options: a girl and her rival
hikers trapped by a blizzard
a student worried about a test
two brothers arguing

questions.stem: What usually happens in the falling action?
options: the problem begins and the characters meet it for the first time
the title appears at the top of the text and the page
characters are introduced to the readers of the story at the start
the effects of the climax unfold and the story moves toward the end

questions.stem: In a story, a team is losing until the last second, when the hero scores. This moment is the—
options: setting
resolution
climax
exposition

questions.stem: Why might an author delay the climax with many complications?
options: to make the story boring for the reader
to remove conflict from the whole plot
to avoid a resolution in the last page
to increase suspense and reader investment

questions.stem: A story ends without fully solving the problem. What is this kind of ending called?
options: a climax at the high point
a rising action before it
an open (unresolved) ending
an exposition at the start

questions.stem: How can a story's resolution reveal its theme?
options: it describes the setting of the story and the weather there at night
it lists the characters in the story one by one in a long row
how the conflict is solved shows what the character or reader learns
it repeats the title of the story at the end of the last page

questions.stem: A character's internal conflict about fear is resolved when she helps a friend despite being scared. What does this resolution show?
options: friends are not important in a story
courage means acting despite fear
she was never afraid of anything
fear always wins in the end

questions.stem: Which change would most raise the stakes in a conflict?
options: the hero has only one hour to save the town
the hero reads a book in the library for an hour
the hero takes a nap on the sofa after the lunch
the hero eats lunch with his friends in the town

questions.stem: What is a line in a poem?
options: the whole poem
one row of words
the title
a chapter

questions.stem: What is the theme of a poem?
options: its rhyme and rhythm pattern
its length and number of lines
its title only, on the first page
its main message or lesson

questions.stem: Which line has rhyme?
options: "A big dog / jumped"
"The sun / is hot"
"The cat sat / on a mat"
"The cat ran / to the house"

questions.stem: A poem describes a tree that bends in storms but never breaks. What might the theme be?
options: leaves are green in the spring
staying strong in hard times
storms are fun for every child
trees are tall and very old

questions.stem: What is rhythm in poetry?
options: the author's name on the cover
the number of pages in the book
the color of the page of the book
the beat or pattern of sounds

questions.stem: A poem has a problem: a bird cannot find its nest. What is this?
options: the rhyme
the poem's conflict
the title
the stanza

questions.stem: A poem shows a child afraid of the dark who learns stars light the way. How is the conflict resolved?
options: the child runs away from home at night
the child stays afraid of the dark forever
the child finds comfort in the stars
the stars disappear and the sky stays black

questions.stem: How do images in a poem help develop its theme?
options: they are random pictures with no link to the topic
they replace the title and the name of the poet
they make the poem longer and harder to read
they create pictures that carry the poem's message

questions.stem: What is the difference between a poem's topic and its theme?
options: they are the same thing, so one word can replace the other
the topic is the rhyme; the theme is the meter of the lines
the topic is what it's about; the theme is the message about it
the theme is the title; the topic is the poet's name

questions.stem: A poem repeats "Keep going" at the end of each stanza. What does the repetition emphasize?
options: sleep
colors
food
perseverance

questions.stem: Which element creates the mood of a poem most?
options: the author's age and home
the font that the poem uses
page numbers at the base
word choice and imagery

questions.stem: A poem contrasts a busy city with a quiet garden where the speaker finds peace. What theme does this contrast suggest?
options: the speaker dislikes plants and does not want a garden
gardens are noisy and full of people who shout
peace can be found by stepping away from noise and hurry
cities are always bad places for people to live in

questions.stem: How can a poem's structure reflect its conflict?
options: the title changes on every page of the poem
only rhyme shows conflict, and line length never matters
lines may grow shorter and choppier as tension rises
structure never matters, because only the words tell the story

questions.stem: A poem ends with a question instead of an answer. What effect does this have on the theme?
options: it gives a clear lesson to the reader of the poem at last
it invites readers to reflect and find their own answer
it repeats the title in the last line of the poem
it ruins the poem and the theme for all readers of it

questions.stem: In a poem, the speaker's conflict is between remembering a lost friend and moving on. Which line best shows resolution?
options: "I keep your laugh, and walk into the light."
"I miss you every night."
"The rain will never stop."
"Why did you go?"
questions.why: It balances memory and moving on.

questions.stem: Which approach best determines a poem's theme?
options: examine how the speaker changes and what images repeat
count the rhymes in each line of the poem and add them up
look at the title only and nothing else in the poem
check the page number of the poem in the book first

questions.stem: Who is the speaker of a poem?
options: the reader who opens the book
the voice telling the poem
the illustrator of the book
the publisher of the poem
questions.why: The speaker is the poem's voice.

questions.stem: A poem says, "I am a tiny seed under the ground." Who is the speaker?
options: a seed
the sun
a farmer
a bird

questions.stem: Is the speaker always the poet?
options: no, the speaker can be a character or object
only in rhymes that are short and silly, never in other poems
yes, always, in every poem that you read in class
only in long poems that have many verses and lines

questions.stem: Which word shows the speaker is talking about themselves?
options: he
I
it
they

questions.stem: A poem is written from a cat's point of view. What might it describe?
options: naps in the sun and chasing mice
cooking dinner in the kitchen all night
doing homework at a desk after school
driving a car to the shops in town

questions.stem: What does a speaker's viewpoint mean?
options: the rhyme at the end of each line of the poem
the title at the top of the page of the poem
the poem's length in lines and in words
how the speaker sees or feels about the subject

questions.stem: A speaker says, "The old house creaks with stories no one hears." How does the speaker feel about the house?
options: it holds forgotten memories worth noticing
it is noisy and annoying only, so no one wants it
it is new and has nothing to say
it is boring and empty of stories

questions.stem: Which detail reveals a speaker is a child?
options: "I voted today."
"My feet don't reach the floor in Grandpa's chair."
"I drove to work."
"I paid the bills."

questions.stem: How can a reader identify a speaker's attitude?
options: by looking at word choice and tone
by counting stanzas in the poem
by the font of the text and its size
by the title only, and nothing else

questions.stem: A poem is spoken by a river to the town. Why might the poet choose this speaker?
options: to make it shorter and easier to read aloud
to show the town from nature's point of view
to make it rhyme at the end of each line
rivers always speak to the people in the towns
questions.why: An unusual speaker offers new perspective.

questions.stem: Which line shows a speaker who is hopeful?
options: "Why try at all?"
"Nothing will ever grow."
"The garden is dead."
"Tomorrow, the seeds will rise."

questions.stem: A speaker describes a war memorial calmly, but the last line says, "and still I cannot read their names." What does this reveal?
options: the speaker cannot read, even a little
the names are missing from the monument
hidden grief beneath the calm description
the speaker is bored by the ceremony

questions.stem: How does a shift in a speaker's viewpoint affect a poem's meaning?
options: it changes the title and also the name of the poet
it shows the speaker has learned or changed, deepening the theme
it has no effect on the meaning, the theme or the mood
it makes the poem confusing only, and nothing else ever changes

questions.stem: Two poems describe the same storm: one speaker is a farmer, the other a child. How might their viewpoints differ?
options: they are identical in all of their words and ideas about the weather
neither notices the storm in the sky above the field
both describe only the sky, and the clouds, and the wind
the farmer worries about crops; the child may feel excitement or fear

questions.stem: What is a dramatic monologue?
options: a play with many actors who speak to each other all the time on a big stage
a short definition of a word that you find in a dictionary or a glossary
a list of rhymes that poets use at the end of their lines in a poem
a poem in which a character speaks to a silent listener, revealing themselves

questions.stem: A speaker praises a king so much that it sounds false. What might the poet be suggesting?
options: the speaker may be afraid or the praise is ironic
the king is perfect and everyone loves him
the speaker is the king himself, hidden in disguise
the poem is a fact report about the king

sets.skill: Purpose of Signs, Posters and Directions

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a STOP sign?
options: to sell cars to drivers
to tell a long tale
to tell drivers to stop
to name a street here

questions.stem: A poster says "Book Fair Friday!" What is its purpose?
options: to warn of danger on the road ahead
to give a recipe for a fruit cake
to tell people about an event
to explain math to young students

questions.stem: Why does a sign say "Wet Floor"?
options: to warn people so they don't slip
to sell mops to the people in the shop
to name the room for visitors
to decorate the floor for the guests

questions.stem: A sign on a door says "Push." What does it tell you?
options: how to open the door
the time it will open
the price of the room
who lives there now

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of directions on a game box?
options: to tell a long story
to list the factory workers
to show prices in a shop
to explain how to play

questions.stem: A poster shows a lost cat with a phone number. What is the purpose?
options: to teach children about cats
to warn people about angry cats nearby
to ask people to help find the cat
to sell a cat to a new owner

questions.stem: Why do warning signs often use red and big letters?
options: to confuse people who pass by
to look pretty on the wall
to grab attention quickly
to save paint for later signs

questions.stem: A poster says "Join the Science Club — Make Things Explode (Safely)!" What is its specific purpose?
options: to warn of explosions in the school lab
to teach chemistry to the children
to sell tickets for the science show
to persuade students to join the club

questions.stem: Which sign gives information rather than a command?
options: Library open 8 a.m.–4 p.m.
Stop at the red light now
Keep out of this room!
No running in the hall

questions.stem: Directions to a museum list turns and landmarks. What is the purpose?
options: to describe the art in the museum
to sell tickets at the front door
to help someone get there
to tell the history of the building

questions.stem: Why might a sign use a picture instead of words?
options: words are not allowed on signs in most public places
pictures are cheaper than words for the sign maker
so people who cannot read the language still understand
to make it longer so the sign takes up more room

questions.stem: A poster for a charity run shows smiling families and says "Every step helps a child." What technique supports its purpose?
options: an emotional appeal that connects running to helping
a warning that tells people to stay away from the race
a map that shows where the race will take place
a list of facts about running and about its history

questions.stem: A sign says "Fine $200 for littering." How does it try to achieve its purpose?
options: by giving directions to the nearest park
by telling a story about a boy and a bag
by praising clean parks and kind people
by warning of a penalty to stop littering

questions.stem: Why might the same message be written differently on a road sign and a website?
options: road signs need long sentences so drivers can study them
a road sign must be read in seconds, so it is short
they never differ, because a message is always the same
websites are illegal in some countries, so they differ

questions.stem: Which change would make a fire-exit sign less effective?
options: placing it above the door
adding a running-person symbol
writing it in small gray letters
lighting it up

questions.stem: A poster lists an event's date but not its location. What does this show about evaluating a poster?
options: dates are unimportant on a poster, so people do not need to read them
check whether it gives all the information needed for its purpose
posters never need locations for people to find them
posters are always complete when they have a picture

sets.skill: Reading a Story vs. Hearing or Viewing It

questions.stem: When you listen to an audiobook, what helps you understand feelings?
options: the reader's voice
the page numbers
the font
the cover

questions.stem: What can a movie show quickly that a book describes with many words?
options: the glossary
the page count
what a place looks like
the author's thoughts about writing

questions.stem: When reading a book yourself, you can—
options: watch special effects in a film
see actors on a stage
go back and reread a part
hear music from a band

questions.stem: Which version lets you imagine the characters' faces yourself?
options: watching the movie
seeing the play
reading the book
looking at the poster

questions.stem: What might an audiobook add to a scary story?
options: a map of the place and its roads in the town
a glossary of the scary words at the end of it
pictures of the monster in color on the screen
spooky sound effects and a tense voice

questions.stem: Why might a movie leave out parts of a book?
options: to fit the story into a shorter time
because books are wrong about the story
to add more pages to the film
to change the title of the book

questions.stem: In the book, a character's thoughts are described; in the film, the actor only frowns. What is lost?
options: the detailed inner thoughts
the title of the book on the cover
the plot of the whole story
the setting of the scene

questions.stem: How can music in a film change how viewers feel about a scene compared with reading it?
options: it has no effect on what the viewers feel
it changes the words that the characters say
it removes all feeling from the whole scene
it can make the scene feel scarier or sadder

questions.stem: Which experience gives the most control over pacing?
options: listening to a live play
watching a movie in a theater
hearing a radio show
reading the text

questions.stem: A narrator in an audiobook uses different voices for each character. How does this help listeners?
options: they can tell who is speaking
it makes the story shorter
it shows pictures
it removes dialogue

questions.stem: Why might two readers picture a book's setting differently but see the same setting in a film?
options: films have no settings
readers don't imagine
books have pictures on every page
the film shows one director's version

questions.stem: A story's twist is hinted at in the narrator's word choice, but the film reveals it through a camera angle. What does this show?
options: the book has no twist, because only films can have them
camera angles are unimportant to a story in any film
the film copied the words of the book exactly as written
each medium uses its own tools to create the same effect

questions.stem: Which question best compares reading and viewing a story?
options: Who printed the book, in which city was it made, and in what year was that?
Which one is longer, the film or the text, when we count all the minutes and the pages?
Which one is cheaper to buy, the film ticket or the book from the shop in town?
How do the film's sound and images change my experience of the climax compared with the text?

questions.stem: Why might a reader feel more connected to a first-person narrator in a book than to the same character on screen?
options: books are louder than films, so readers listen closely
screens are smaller than books, so they are harder to see
films have no characters, so there is nobody to follow
the book shares the character's thoughts directly

questions.stem: A radio drama relies only on sound. How must it convey setting?
options: through subtitles at the bottom of the screen
through sound effects, dialogue and narration
it cannot, because there is nothing to see
through pictures and drawings on the stage
questions.why: Sound must do all the work.

questions.stem: What is a benefit of experiencing the same story in several media?
options: you notice how each medium shapes meaning and deepen your understanding
the stories become identical in every way, so you never need to compare them
nothing changes because every medium tells it the same way
you can skip reading the book and just watch the film instead

questions.stem: What is rhetoric?
options: the art of using language to persuade or inform
a music instrument played in an orchestra
a type of math used to count large numbers
a science lab where students do experiments daily

questions.stem: A famous speech repeats "We can" many times. Why?
options: to confuse the listeners on purpose
the speaker forgot the words of the speech
to inspire and make the message memorable
to fill time before the end of the speech

questions.stem: What is a seminal text?
options: a short joke told in a class by a teacher
a grocery list for the weekend at home
a recipe for a cake or for some bread
an important, influential document or speech

questions.stem: Why do leaders give speeches during hard times?
options: to unite and encourage people
to tell jokes and make people laugh
to read the news only, line by line
to sell products to the people

questions.stem: Which is a rhetorical question?
options: "Did you eat lunch?"
"What time is it?"
"Who among us does not want a better future?"
"Where is the library?"

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a nation's founding documents?
options: to set out rights, laws and principles
to list sports scores for each team
to entertain children with stories
to sell land to new settlers there

questions.stem: A speech says, "Ask not what your team can do for you; ask what you can do for your team." What technique is this?
options: a statistic that gives a number from a survey
a definition of a hard word, as in a dictionary
a simile that compares two things with like
reversal of word order for emphasis (antimetabole)

questions.stem: Why might a speaker refer to shared history or values?
options: to waste time before the end of the talk
to confuse listeners with long old stories
to show off how much history he knows
to connect with the audience and build unity

questions.stem: Which appeal uses facts and logic?
options: logos
humor
ethos
pathos

questions.stem: A speech describes children who cannot go to school. Which appeal is this?
options: pathos (emotion)
logos (logic)
ethos (credibility)
none

questions.stem: Why do historic speeches often use parallel structure and triads (groups of three)?
options: they create rhythm and make ideas memorable
they hide meaning from the audience
they make speeches shorter and easier to give
they are required by law in many countries

questions.stem: A founding document lists grievances against a ruler. What is the rhetorical purpose?
options: to praise the ruler for all of his good work
to tell a story for fun to the citizens
to justify a decision by showing many reasons
to list sports rules for the new teams in town

questions.stem: How can a speaker's acknowledgment of opponents strengthen a seminal speech?
options: it adds humor to the speech, so that the crowd laughs a lot
it weakens the speech every time, because it makes the speaker look weak
it shows fairness and makes the call to action more credible
it changes the topic of the speech to something else for a while

questions.stem: Why might the meaning of a seminal text be debated for centuries?
options: its broad language can be applied to new situations
it is too short to have any real meaning
it has no meaning, so people just like to argue about it
it was never read, so nobody knows what it says

questions.stem: Which sentence analyzes rhetoric rather than summarizing?
options: The speech happened in a big city, and many people came to the hall to hear it, young and old.
The speaker talked about time and about the days of the week, and he named each one.
The speech was long, and it lasted for almost two hours in the hall, so many people left early.
By repeating "now is the time," the speaker builds urgency that pushes listeners to act.

questions.stem: Your friend trips and says, "Well, that was graceful." What is this?
options: a fact
a question
sarcasm
a rhyme

questions.stem: A huge storm destroys a fence and someone says, "We had a little wind." What is this?
options: a simile
exaggeration
understatement
a question

questions.stem: What is satire?
options: a science report about the weather and the four seasons
a sad poem about the sea and the sky above the town
a list of rules for a game played in the school yard
humor that makes fun of people or society to show a problem

questions.stem: Which sentence is sarcastic?
options: "Oh great, more homework. My favorite!" groaned Ali.
Homework is due Monday morning, said Ali, and he wrote it in his book.
Ali likes math more than anything else at school.
Ali finished his homework early, before dinner, and he went out.

questions.stem: Why do people use sarcasm?
options: to joke or show annoyance by saying the opposite
to give exact directions to a place in the town
to list facts and numbers about a topic
to define the hard words in a school text

questions.stem: Which is an understatement about a marathon?
options: "It was the longest race ever!"
"I ran all day and night!"
"It was 42 kilometers long."
"It was a bit of a walk."

questions.stem: A cartoon shows a man buying a giant car to drive two blocks to the gym. What is the satire criticizing?
options: gyms
exercise
wasteful habits
cars being blue

questions.stem: How can you tell a statement is sarcastic in writing?
options: it is always very long, with many words in a row
it has a question mark at the end of it
the context shows the speaker means the opposite
it uses capital letters only, all through the line

questions.stem: A doctor says a broken leg is "just a scratch." What effect does the understatement create?
options: humor or calm by downplaying a serious injury
fear and panic among the people who hear it
a definition of a leg in a medical book
a precise diagnosis that the doctor must write

questions.stem: Which is the best example of satire?
options: a real weather report that tells people about rain and wind
a math textbook that teaches students how to add numbers
a fake news story about a city banning walking to reduce traffic
a recipe for cake that lists the flour, eggs and sugar to buy

questions.stem: Why might sarcasm be misunderstood in text messages?
options: readers can't hear the tone of voice
texts are too long to read quickly
texts have no words in them at all
sarcasm is always obvious to every reader

questions.stem: A satirical essay suggests solving traffic by banning cars on weekdays and walking on weekends. What is its likely real purpose?
options: to criticize poor planning by proposing absurd solutions
to actually ban walking in the city so people use cars
to describe cars and how they work for readers
to teach geography and the names of cities and roads

questions.stem: How does understatement work in "The war was a little inconvenient for the villagers"?
options: it praises the war and shows that the soldiers were kind
it is a simple fact about the village and its people
it accurately describes the war and the people who lived there
it shocks readers by downplaying terrible suffering

questions.stem: What distinguishes satire from simple insults?
options: satire uses humor and exaggeration to point to a larger problem
insults are always funny and never hurt anyone's feelings at all
satire is always gentle and never points out any problem
satire has no target and never talks about real people

questions.stem: A character says "Lovely day" while standing in a flood, and the narrator notes his trembling hands. What does this show?
options: the sarcasm hides real fear
he is joking happily with his friends
the day is sunny and warm
he loves floods more than anything

questions.stem: Why can satire be powerful in a society where open criticism is risky?
options: it avoids all the topics of the day
satire is always ignored by the public
it uses facts only, with no humor at all
humor can carry criticism indirectly

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: I need: paper pens and glue, please, now.
I: need three things for school, today.
I need three things: paper, pens and glue.
I need three: things for my class, today.
questions.why: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The rain; stopped we went outside.
The rain stopped we; went outside.
The rain stopped; we went outside.
The; rain stopped.

questions.stem: Where do you use a colon in time?
options: at the end of a sentence, like a full stop
before a name, like in a letter
after the year, like in a date
between hours and minutes, like 3:15

questions.stem: Which greeting in a business letter uses a colon?
options: Dear Principal Ahmed:
Dear: Principal Ahmed
Dear Principal Ahmed.
Dear Principal Ahmed;
questions.why: Formal letters may use a colon.

questions.stem: A semicolon can replace—
options: an apostrophe
a question mark
a comma and a joining word like and
a period at the end of a paragraph

questions.stem: Which punctuation mark looks like two dots?
options: a colon
a semicolon
a comma
a dash

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semicolon before a transition correctly?
options: I studied hard, therefore; I passed.
I studied hard therefore, I passed.
I studied hard; therefore, I passed.
I studied; hard therefore I passed.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a colon to introduce an explanation?
options: There was: one reason we lost the game last night.
There was one reason we lost: we didn't practice.
There: was one reason we lost it, I think.
There was one: reason we lost the game, I think.

questions.stem: Which is a run-on that a semicolon could fix?
options: The bus was late we missed the movie.
Because the bus was late, we missed it.
We missed the movie, and we went home.
The bus was late again, as it often is.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a colon incorrectly?
options: My favorite colors are: blue and green.
She said one word: wow.
Remember this: be kind.
I have two favorite colors: blue and green.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses semicolons in a list with commas?
options: We visited Paris, France, Rome, Italy, Cairo, Egypt;
We visited Paris; France, Rome; Italy.
We visited; Paris France Rome Italy.
We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Cairo, Egypt.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a colon to introduce a quotation formally?
options: The coach's: advice was simply "Never give up."
The coach said: never give up, my friends.
The coach's advice was simple: "Never give up."
The: coach said "Never give up" to us.
questions.why: A complete sentence before the colon.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly joins the clauses? "The experiment failed, the hypothesis was wrong."
options: The experiment failed: and the hypothesis was wrong.
The experiment; failed the hypothesis was wrong.
The experiment failed, and; the hypothesis was wrong.
The experiment failed; the hypothesis was wrong.
questions.why: A semicolon fixes the comma splice.

questions.stem: When is a colon better than a semicolon between two clauses?
options: never, because the two marks do the same job
when the second clause explains or expands the first
when the clauses are unrelated to each other
when listing names only, such as friends in class

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The forecast: was clear rain all week; picnic.
The forecast was; clear: rain.
The forecast was clear: rain all week; the picnic was canceled.
The forecast was clear; rain all week: the picnic was canceled.

questions.stem: Why do writers use semicolons instead of periods between closely related ideas?
options: to make sentences end sooner than they should
to show the ideas are strongly connected
to add a list at the end of a line
to ask questions in the middle of a text

questions.stem: What is the setting of a story?
options: the main character of the tale
where and when it happens
the problem the hero must solve
the ending of the story

questions.stem: What is mood?
options: the author's name on the cover of the book
the title at the top of the page of the story
the setting of the story only, and its time
the feeling the reader gets from the story

questions.stem: "The dark forest was silent except for an owl's hoot." What mood is created?
options: bored
mysterious or spooky
